metadata.scope: e_deccan (231 baronies across k_andhra, k_karnata, k_lanka, k_maharastra, k_tamilakam, k_telingana)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding (stripped of key prefixes and parenthetical notes).
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier extracted from modern_name; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.anachronism_type: Mutually exclusive historicity category: attested_pre_867 | fictional_placeholder | post_867_eponym | renamed_post_867 | modern_anachronism | early_modern_foundation | high_late_medieval_attestation | unattested_indigenous_or_minor.
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= that bookmark year.
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation for the audited name (negative values = BCE; null if unattested).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.eponym: Structured eponym object {year, post_867, type, details} when named after a person, saint, ruler, deity, or dynasty/tribe; null otherwise.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.historical_names: List of distinct pre-867 attested names for the same site or immediate predecessor: [{name, native_script, language, attested_from, attested_to, source, relationship, notes}].
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_ittagi.first_mention_attestation: 1112 CE Kannada and Sanskrit stone inscription at the Mahadeva Temple in Ittagi (recorded as Ittage in the Nareyamgal-12 division of Belvola-300), erected by Dandanayaka Mahadeva under Western Chalukya Emperor Vikramaditya VI.
b_ittagi.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Kannada 'ittage' (brick, ultimately from Sanskrit 'ishtaka'), designating the temple settlement in Koppal district famous for its 1112 CE Western Chalukya Mahadeva Temple.

b_sriparvata.first_mention_attestation: Ikshvaku dynasty Prakrit and Sanskrit Brahmi inscriptions at Nagarjunakonda (c. 250–275 CE), which refer to the hill range as Sriparvata (Siripavvata).
b_sriparvata.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound 'śrī-parvata' meaning 'sacred mountain', attested in 3rd-century CE Ikshvaku epigraphy for the Nallamala hills near Nagarjunakonda and Srisailam.

b_mudivemu.first_mention_attestation: 11th-century CE Eastern Chalukya copper-plate inscriptions (from the reign of Rajaraja Narendra, c. 1022 CE onward), which record the dynastic origin legend set at Mudivemu (modern Peddamudium).
b_mudivemu.etymology_analysis: Telugu toponym combining 'mudi' (old) with 'vemu' (neem, or a Dravidian settlement suffix), later distinguished as Peddamudium.

b_ahobalam.first_mention_attestation: 14th-century CE temple records and Reddi-period inscriptions at Upper Ahobilam; later Vijayanagara inscriptions (e.g., 1472 CE) also attest the site.
b_ahobalam.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound 'aho-balam' ('what great power!'), traditionally linked to the Devas' exclamation upon witnessing Narasimha's strength; also interpreted with 'bilam' (cave).

b_amaravati.first_mention_attestation: Late 18th-century CE founding of the town of Amaravati (c. 1796–1797 CE) by Zamindar Vasireddy Venkatadri Naidu around the Amaresvara Shiva temple adjacent to ancient Dhanyakataka (Dharanikota).
b_amaravati.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit 'Amaravati' ('abode of the immortals'), adopted for the modern town around the Amaresvara Shiva temple in the late 18th century CE on the site of ancient Buddhist and Satavahana Dhanyakataka.

historical_names.name: Dhanyakataka
historical_names.source: Early Brahmi inscriptions at the Amaravati Mahachaitya (c. 2nd century BCE – 2nd century CE) and Xuanzang's Si-Yu-Ki (c. 640 CE)
historical_names.notes: The ancient Satavahana and Buddhist metropolis at the site was attested as Dhanyakataka (Prakrit Dhamnakada, modern Dharanikota) from early Brahmi inscriptions through the 7th-century CE travelogue of Xuanzang and medieval Kota inscriptions.

historical_names.name: Dhamnakada
historical_names.source: Early Brahmi inscriptions at the Amaravati Mahachaitya (c. 2nd century BCE – 2nd century CE) and Xuanzang's Si-Yu-Ki (c. 640 CE)
historical_names.notes: The ancient Satavahana and Buddhist metropolis at the site was attested as Dhanyakataka (Prakrit Dhamnakada, modern Dharanikota) from early Brahmi inscriptions through the 7th-century CE travelogue of Xuanzang and medieval Kota inscriptions.

b_pondugala.first_mention_attestation: Stone inscription at Pondugala, Palnad Taluk, Guntur District, dated Saka 1672 (1750 CE) in South Indian Inscriptions Vol. 40.
b_pondugala.etymology_analysis: Telugu village toponym in Palnadu with the characteristic '-gala' / '-galla' settlement suffix.

b_addanki.first_mention_attestation: Addanki poetic inscription (Pandaranga inscription) of 848 CE, issued by Pandaranga, army chief of Eastern Chalukya king Gunaga Vijayaditya III.
b_addanki.etymology_analysis: Old Telugu toponym attested in the 848 CE Pandaranga inscription, linked to Telugu 'aḍḍam' (barrier/across).

b_udayagiri.first_mention_attestation: 1343 CE stone inscription near Buggabavi at Udayagiri recording temple grants by Kampana I (brother of Harihara I) of the Sangama dynasty of Vijayanagara, administering the province of Udayagiri-rajya.
b_udayagiri.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound 'udaya-giri' ('sunrise hill' or 'eastern mountain'), naming the strategic hill fortress in Nellore district, Andhra Pradesh.

b_nilagiri.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE epigraphy or classical sources for a settlement in coastal Andhra Pradesh.

b_bhairavunikonda.first_mention_attestation: Rock-cut Shiva cave temples at Bhairavakona date stylistically to the 7th–8th century CE, but the modern Telugu name Bhairavunikonda is unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE inscriptions.

morphemes.translation: of Bhairava (a fierce form of Shiva)

b_bhairavunikonda.etymology_analysis: Telugu possessive compound meaning 'hill of Bhairava', referring to the Kala Bhairava shrine at the Nallamala rock-cut cave complex.

b_mutfili.first_mention_attestation: Travelogue of Marco Polo (c. 1292 CE), who referred to the Kakatiya port of Motupalli (first epigraphically attested as Motupalli in Ganapatideva's 1244–1245 CE charter) as Mutfili.
b_mutfili.etymology_analysis: European/Venetian rendering by Marco Polo (c. 1292 CE) of Telugu 'Mōṭupalli' ('settlement on the mound/coast').

b_pithapuram.first_mention_attestation: Samudragupta's Allahabad Pillar Inscription (Prayaga Prashasti, c. 350 CE), which records the defeat of King Mahendragiri of Pishtapura (Mahendragiri-Pishtapuraka), later corroborated by Pulakeshin II's Aihole Inscription (634 CE).

morphemes.translation: sacred seat, altar (re-etymologized from earlier piṣṭa 'crushed/stronghold')

b_pithapuram.etymology_analysis: Modern Telugu-Sanskrit evolution of ancient Pishtapura ('stronghold/flour-city'), attested in 4th-century CE Gupta and 7th-century CE Chalukya epigraphy and later re-etymologized as Pithapuram ('city of the sacred seat/Shakti Peetha').

b_rajamahendravaram.first_mention_attestation: Founded by Eastern Chalukya king Ammaraja I (r. 919–934 CE), and later prominent under Rajaraja Narendra (r. 1022–1061 CE).

eponym.details: Named Rajamahendrapuram / Rajamahendravaram after the 10th–11th century Eastern Chalukya rulers (Ammaraja I, r. 919–934 CE, titled Rajamahendra, and Rajaraja Narendra, r. 1022–1061 CE).

morphemes.translation: great king / royal title of Ammaraja I
boon, gift, or adaptation of Sanskrit puram (city)

b_rajamahendravaram.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Rājamahendrapuram' ('city of King Mahendra'), Teluguized as 'Rājamahendravaram' and anglicized as Rajahmundry.

b_draksharama.first_mention_attestation: Inscription from the reign of Eastern Chalukya king Amma II (r. 945–970 CE) at the Bhimeswara temple in Draksharamam (traditionally attributed to Chalukya Bhima I, r. 888–918 CE).
b_draksharama.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Dakṣārāma' ('abode/garden of Daksha'), Sanskritized/altered in Telugu as Draksharamam.

b_vengipura.first_mention_attestation: Salankayana dynasty copper-plate inscriptions (4th–5th century CE, c. 350 CE onward), nine of which were issued from Vengipura (modern Pedavegi).
b_vengipura.etymology_analysis: Sanskritized compound 'Veṅgipura' ('city of Vengi'), capital of the Salankayana, Vishnukundina, and Eastern Chalukya dynasties.

b_vijayawada.first_mention_attestation: Account of Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Xuanzang (c. 640 CE), who stayed in Bezawada (Vijayawada), followed by 9th-century CE Eastern Chalukya inscriptions at Malleswara temple.
b_vijayawada.etymology_analysis: Compound of Sanskrit 'vijaya' (victory) and Telugu 'vāḍa' (place/quarter), also historically known as Bezawada.

b_polavaram.first_mention_attestation: Vilasa Copper Plate grant of Musunuri Prolaya Nayaka (1325 CE), recording that the donee Vennaya renamed the village Vilasa to Prolavaram after King Prola.

eponym.details: Named Prolavaram (modern Polavaram) after Musunuri Prolaya Nayaka (r. c. 1325–1333 CE), who granted the village of Vilasa in 1325 CE.

morphemes.translation: Prola (personal name of Musunuri Prolaya Nayaka)

b_polavaram.etymology_analysis: From Telugu 'Prōla-varam' ('gift/boon of Prola'), coined in 1325 CE in honor of Musunuri Prolaya Nayaka and later shortened to Polavaram.

b_dwarasamudra.first_mention_attestation: 11th-century CE Hoysala inscriptions beginning c. 1062 CE under King Vinayaditya, recording Dorasamudra (Dwarasamudra, modern Halebidu) as the Hoysala royal capital.
b_dwarasamudra.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound 'dvāra-samudra' ('gateway to the ocean/reservoir', vernacular Dorasamudra), referring to the large royal irrigation tank around which the Hoysala capital of Halebidu was built.

b_shravana_belgola.first_mention_attestation: Early Old Kannada Jain nisidhi inscriptions on Chandragiri Hill at Shravanabelagola dating to c. 600 CE (7th century CE).
b_shravana_belgola.etymology_analysis: Compound of Sanskrit 'śravaṇa' (Jain monk) and Kannada 'beḷ-koḷa' ('white pond'), referring to the sacred tank between Indragiri and Chandragiri hills.

b_sosavur.first_mention_attestation: 11th-century CE Hoysala inscriptions recording Sosevur (modern Angadi) as the earliest Hoysala capital (1026–1048 CE).
b_sosavur.etymology_analysis: Old Kannada toponym ending in '-ūr' (settlement/town), the ancestral home of the Hoysala dynasty.

b_manyapura.first_mention_attestation: Western Ganga inscriptions of King Sripurusha (r. 726–788 CE; capital shifted to Manyapura/Manne around 731 CE).
b_manyapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit 'Mānyapura' ('honorable city'), corresponding to Kannada 'Manne', the 8th-century Western Ganga royal capital.

b_nandagiri.first_mention_attestation: Inscriptions of Hoysala king Veera Ramanatha (r. 1263–1297 CE) and Ballala III (1301 CE), naming Kundani (Hesar-Kundani) as Ramanatha's royal residence.
b_nandagiri.etymology_analysis: Medieval Kannada toponym attested in 13th-century Hoysala inscriptions as the seat of the Kundani kingdom.

b_srirangapatna.first_mention_attestation: Early 12th-century CE Hoysala inscriptions at Melukote (Epigraphia Carnatica Vol. III) from the reign of Vishnuvardhana and the residence of philosopher Ramanujacharya (c. 1098–1120 CE), attesting the sacred hill of Yadugiri / Yadavagiri.
b_srirangapatna.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit oronym 'Yadu-giri' ('Yadu Hill', also Yadavagiri), the classical sacred name of the rocky hills at Melukote in Mandya district, Karnataka.

b_belapura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE epigraphy or classical sources.

b_talakad.first_mention_attestation: Early Western Ganga dynasty records and inscriptions from the reign of Harivarma (c. 390 CE), when Talakadu (Sanskrit Dalavanapura) became the Ganga capital.
b_talakad.etymology_analysis: Kannada compound 'Tala-kāḍu' (traditionally associated with 'forest of palms' or 'Tala's forest'), Sanskritized in early Ganga records as Dalavanapura.

b_mercara.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1681 CE when Haleri king Muddu Raja moved his capital to Madikeri (anglicized under British rule as Mercara).

eponym.details: Anglicization of Madikeri (originally Muddu-raja-keri), named after the 17th-century Haleri ruler Muddu Raja who established it as his capital in 1681 CE.

b_mercara.etymology_analysis: Mercara is the British colonial anglicization of Madikeri, contracted from 'Muddu-rāja-kēri' ('town/quarter of Muddu Raja', 1681 CE).

b_moyar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a settlement name in pre-867 CE epigraphy; refers to the Moyar River valley between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
b_moyar.etymology_analysis: Dravidian hydronym (also spelled Mayar) combining a Dravidian root with 'ār' (river), designating the tributary of the Bhavani River.

b_seringapatam.first_mention_attestation: Named after the Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple at Srirangapatna, consecrated around 984 CE; later anglicized as Seringapatam.
b_seringapatam.etymology_analysis: Colonial anglicization of 'Śrīraṅgapaṭṭaṇa' ('city of Lord Ranganatha'), named for the Ranganathaswamy Temple consecrated c. 984 CE.

b_kalyani.first_mention_attestation: Established as the royal capital of the Western Chalukyas by Someshvara I around 1050 CE (Kalyana / Kalyani, modern Basavakalyan).
b_kalyani.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit 'Kalyāṇī' ('the auspicious city'), capital of the Later/Western Chalukyas from c. 1050 CE.

b_manyakheta.first_mention_attestation: Capital of the Rashtrakuta Empire from 814 CE under Emperor Amoghavarsha I (r. 814–878 CE), attested in 9th-century Rashtrakuta inscriptions.

b_bidar.first_mention_attestation: Inscriptions found during excavations around Bidar Fort dating back to the 10th century CE during the Western Chalukya period (974–1190 CE).
b_bidar.etymology_analysis: Derived from Kannada 'bidiru' (bamboo), referring to the bamboo groves in the region; also linked in tradition to ancient Vidura.

b_gulbarga.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Gulbarga in 1321 CE following the annexation of Kalburgi by the Delhi Sultanate.
b_gulbarga.etymology_analysis: Persianized reinterpretation ('city of flower gardens', from 'gul' + 'bāgh') of the earlier Kannada name Kalburgi ('rocky land').

historical_names.name: Kalburgi
historical_names.source: 6th-century CE Chalukya records
historical_names.notes: Attested as Kalburgi ('rocky land' or 'stone fortification' in Kannada) in 6th-century CE Chalukya records before being renamed Gulbarga in 1321 CE.

historical_names.name: Kalaburagi
historical_names.source: 6th-century CE Chalukya records
historical_names.notes: Attested as Kalburgi ('rocky land' or 'stone fortification' in Kannada) in 6th-century CE Chalukya records before being renamed Gulbarga in 1321 CE.

b_sagar.first_mention_attestation: Rashtrakuta inscription of 939 CE at Sirval (reign of Krishna III) mentioning Sagaranadu, and 10th–11th century CE Yadgir Fort inscriptions naming Sagar.
b_sagar.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit 'sāgara' (lake/reservoir or ocean), referring to Dodda Sagar in Yadgir district.

b_bagavi.first_mention_attestation: Kalachuri inscription of Rayamurari Sovideva at Bagavadi dated 1169 CE (South Indian Inscriptions Vol. XV).
b_bagavi.etymology_analysis: Kannada toponym 'Bāgevāḍi' / 'Bāgavaḍi' ('settlement of bāge trees'), shortened to Bagavi.

b_kembavi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE epigraphy or classical sources.

b_adoni.first_mention_attestation: Raichur Fort stone inscription of Kakatiya commander Gona Vithala dated November 25, 1294 CE (Saka 1216), recording the capture of the fortified town of Adavani (modern Adoni) during Prataparudra II's campaign.
b_adoni.etymology_analysis: Modern contracted form of medieval Adavani (sometimes Sanskritized as Yadavagiri), the historic fortified town in Kurnool district, Andhra Pradesh.

b_vijayanagara.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1336 CE by Harihara I and Bukka Raya I of the Sangama dynasty as the imperial capital of the Vijayanagara Empire on the southern bank of the Tungabhadra River.
b_vijayanagara.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound 'vijaya-nagara' meaning 'City of Victory', coined for the new Sangama imperial capital founded in 1336 CE at Hampi.

historical_names.name: Pampa-tirtha
historical_names.source: Togurshode copper-plate grant of Badami Chalukya King Vinayaditya (689–690 CE)
historical_names.notes: The sacred Tungabhadra river site at Hampi was attested as Pampa-tirtha (Pampa-kshetra) in Badami Chalukya epigraphy from 689 CE, centuries before the founding of Vijayanagara in 1336 CE.

historical_names.name: Pampa-kshetra
historical_names.source: Togurshode copper-plate grant of Badami Chalukya King Vinayaditya (689–690 CE)
historical_names.notes: The sacred Tungabhadra river site at Hampi was attested as Pampa-tirtha (Pampa-kshetra) in Badami Chalukya epigraphy from 689 CE, centuries before the founding of Vijayanagara in 1336 CE.

b_kampili.first_mention_attestation: Mid-11th century CE Chola inscriptions of Rajadhiraja Chola I (c. 1044–1045 CE) and Virarajendra Chola (c. 1068 CE) recording military campaigns against the Western Chalukyas and the sacking of Kampili on the Tungabhadra River.
b_kampili.etymology_analysis: Kannada toponym for the strategic fortified town on the southern bank of the Tungabhadra River in Ballari district, contested in 11th-century Chalukya–Chola wars and later capital of the 14th-century Kampili kingdom.

b_masur.first_mention_attestation: 11th-century CE Western Chalukya and Kadamba feudatory inscriptions from Dharwad-Haveri (Bombay-Karnataka epigraphs) citing Masur as the chief town of the Masur-12 administrative division.
b_masur.etymology_analysis: Old Kannada settlement name ending in '-ūr' (village/town), attested in medieval Western Chalukya inscriptions as the administrative seat of the Masur-12 division in modern Haveri district, Karnataka.

b_shringeri.first_mention_attestation: Earliest concrete epigraphic records are the 1346 CE Vijayanagara grants by Harihara I and Bukka Raya I to Bharati Tirtha at Sringeri; critical historiography (e.g., Hermann Kulke) notes no contemporary <= 867 CE epigraphic evidence for Adi Shankara's traditional c. 800 CE establishment.
b_shringeri.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Śṛṅgagiri' ('Rishyasringa's hill' or 'peaked hill'), contracted to Sringeri (repo: Schringeri).

b_arka.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE epigraphy or classical sources as a settlement in the Banavasi region.

b_kudala.first_mention_attestation: Medieval stone inscriptions at the Sangamesvara/Rameshvara temple complex (e.g., 1160 CE and Hoysala records) at Koodli (Kudali), at the confluence of the Tunga and Bhadra rivers.
b_kudala.etymology_analysis: From Kannada 'kūḍalu' (confluence), referring to the meeting of the Tunga and Bhadra rivers at Koodli (Kudali).

b_gutti.first_mention_attestation: Damaged rock inscriptions near the Narasimha temple inside Gooty Fort (Gutti) from the reign of Western Chalukya king Vikramaditya VI (r. 1076–1126 CE).

b_kandanavolu.first_mention_attestation: Medieval historical records of the Chola and Kakatiya periods (12th–13th centuries CE) referring to Kurnool as Kandanavolu or Kandanolu.
b_kandanavolu.etymology_analysis: Telugu 'Kandanavōlu' (from 'kandana' + 'prōlu'), meaning 'town of cart-greasing' at the Tungabhadra river crossing, later contracted to Kurnool.

b_adavani.first_mention_attestation: Western Chalukya Kannada inscriptions in Adoni taluk (e.g., Pedda Tumbalam 1137 CE and Chinnatumbalam mentioning 'Adavani five-hundred').
b_adavani.etymology_analysis: Medieval Deccan toponym 'Ādavāni' (later contracted to Adoni), attested in Kalyani Chalukya records as the center of Adavani-500.

b_parivi.first_mention_attestation: Associated in historical scholarship with Parigi (Anantapur), traditional capital of the early Bana kings, though no contemporary pre-867 CE inscription directly proves the identification.
b_parivi.etymology_analysis: Toponym 'Parivi' (also Parivipura, identified with modern Parigi), adapted in repo orthography as Pariwi.

b_nidugallu.first_mention_attestation: Became the capital of the Nidugal Cholas in 1196 CE and is attested in the inscription of Irungola II (c. 1232–1280 CE).
b_nidugallu.etymology_analysis: Kannada compound 'Niḍu-gallu' meaning 'lofty rock', referring to the hill fortress of Nidugal.

b_hemavati.first_mention_attestation: Sanskritized name Hemavati attested in later Nolamba-Pallava and medieval records; earlier 9th-century CE Nolamba inscriptions refer to the capital as Henjeru.
b_hemavati.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit 'Hemavatī' ('golden'), a Sanskritization of the older Kannada/Telugu name Henjeru.

historical_names.name: Henjeru
historical_names.source: 9th-century CE Nolamba-Pallava inscriptions
historical_names.notes: Known as Henjeru in 9th-century CE Nolamba-Pallava records before being Sanskritized to Hemavati.

b_uchangidurga.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Uchangi, the capital of the Uchangi Pandyas (e.g., Vijaya Pandya, r. c. 1148–1187 CE) in Nolambavadi.
b_uchangidurga.etymology_analysis: Compound of Kannada 'Uchangi' and Sanskrit 'durga' (hill fort), adapted in repo orthography as Utschangidurge.

b_basavapattana.first_mention_attestation: 16th-century CE records of the Vijayanagara-era Nayakas (prior seat of Hanumappa Nayaka before establishing Tarikere in 1545 CE).

b_honnavalli.first_mention_attestation: 11th-century CE local foundation history attributing the village to Someswararaya of the Harnahalli Nayak family.
b_honnavalli.etymology_analysis: Kannada compound 'Honnu-haḷḷi' ('golden village' or village of goddess Honnu Amma), assimilated to Honnavalli.

b_mudgal.first_mention_attestation: 11th–12th century CE Western Chalukya and Seuna (Yadava) stone inscriptions from Mudgal in Raichur district attesting it as an administrative and educational center in the Raichur Doab.
b_mudgal.etymology_analysis: Kannada toponym combining 'mudu-' (old) with 'kal' (rock/stone, voiced to '-gal'), also linked by local tradition to the Vedic sage Mudgala; a major fortified town in the Raichur Doab.

b_alampur.first_mention_attestation: Western Chalukya inscription of Vikramaditya VI dated 1101 CE mentioning the site as Hatampura (later Halampuram / Alampuram).

b_mushangi.first_mention_attestation: Chola-period inscription at Maski (1020 CE) and Rajendra Chola I's records of the battle against Jayasimha II at Musangi (Masangipura).
b_mushangi.etymology_analysis: Derived from 'Mahāsaṅgha' -> 'Masangipura' -> 'Musangi'/'Mushangi' (modern Maski), adapted in repo orthography as Muschangi.

b_raichur.first_mention_attestation: Raichur Fort built under Kakatiya rule in 1284–1294 CE (with a 1294 CE fort bastion inscription).
b_raichur.etymology_analysis: From Kannada 'Rāyacūru' ('king's town' or 'town of rocks'), anglicized as Raichur.

b_koppam.first_mention_attestation: Amoghavarsha I's Kannada work Kavirajamarga (c. 850 CE), which describes Koppal as 'Vidita Maha Kopana Nagara'.
b_koppam.etymology_analysis: From ancient Kannada 'Kopana' (modern Koppal), also rendered as Koppam in medieval South Indian records.

b_vankapura.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Konnur inscription of Rashtrakuta Emperor Amoghavarsha I (dated Saka 782 / 860 CE), documenting Bankeyarasa (Bankesa) founding/naming Bankapura prior to 867 CE (also cited in the 898 CE Uttarapurana).
b_vankapura.etymology_analysis: Named 'Baṅkāpura' ('city of Bankeya') after the 9th-century Rashtrakuta governor Bankeyarasa; Sanskritized/variant spelling Vankapura.

b_anegandi.first_mention_attestation: Early 14th-century CE Vijayanagara/pre-Vijayanagara records (c. 1334 CE) naming the elephant enclosure on the Tungabhadra as Anegundi.
b_anegandi.etymology_analysis: Kannada compound 'Āne-gundi' meaning 'elephant gorge/enclosure', traditionally associated with the mythical Kishkindha.

b_vaijayanti.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 2nd-century CE Nasik cave inscription of Satavahana king Gautamiputra Satakarni (as lord of Vaijayanti) and the c. 175 CE Chutu dynasty Banavasi/Malavalli inscriptions (Vaijayantipati); Ptolemy (c. 150 CE) also records the city as Banaouasei.

morphemes.translation: victorious / banner of victory (ancient capital name of Banavasi)

b_vaijayanti.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Vaijayantī ('victorious, bearing the banner of victory') was the classical dynastic and epigraphic name of Banavasi, capital of the Chutu and Kadamba dynasties, attested from the 2nd century CE Satavahana and Chutu inscriptions.

b_hubli.first_mention_attestation: First attested in an 11th-century CE inscription at the Bhavani Shankar Temple in old Hubli (Rayara Hubli), which records the settlement as Eleya Purvada Halli ('village of the flowering creeper').
b_hubli.etymology_analysis: Hubli (officially Hubballi) derives from Old Kannada Hūvina Baḷḷi ('flowering creeper'), attested in 11th-century CE Chalukyan-era inscriptions as Eleya Purvada Halli / Purballi.

b_hangal.first_mention_attestation: Attested from c. 969 CE in medieval Kannada and Sanskrit inscriptions of the Kadambas of Hangal as Pānuṅgal / Hānuṅgal (the Hangal-500 province).

morphemes.translation: ancient territorial name (evolving to Hānuṅgal / Hangal)

b_hangal.etymology_analysis: Recorded in 10th-12th century CE epigraphy as Pānuṅgal and Hānuṅgallu, the seat of the Hangal Kadamba branch (c. 969-1347 CE). Later tradition identified it with the epic Virāṭanagara, though contemporary pre-867 CE epigraphic attestation is lacking.

b_vatapi.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 543 CE Badami cliff inscription of Chalukya king Pulakeshin I, which records the fortification of the hill above Vātāpi, and in the 634 CE Aihole inscription of Pulakeshin II.

morphemes.translation: ancient name of Badami (associated with the Puranic demon Vatapi)

b_vatapi.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Vātāpi (modern Badami) served as the royal capital of the Early Chalukyas from 543 CE, named in Puranic tradition after the asura Vatapi subdued by the sage Agastya.

b_kudalasangama.first_mention_attestation: Becomes prominent in the 12th century CE as the site of the samadhi of Veerashaiva/Lingayat founder Basava (c. 1167 CE), with Chalukyan-era temple structures dating to the 11th-12th centuries CE.
b_kudalasangama.etymology_analysis: Bilingual Kannada-Sanskrit compound meaning 'the confluence/junction' (of the Krishna and Malaprabha rivers), famous from the 12th century CE as the sacred Lingayat pilgrimage center.

b_belgaum.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the late 12th century CE under the Ratta dynasty of Saundatti (e.g., 1199 CE pillar inscription of Ratta king Kartaveerya IV and 1204 CE fort construction), when it was known in Sanskrit as Veṇugrāma.
b_belgaum.etymology_analysis: Belgaum (Kannada Belagāvi) derives from Sanskrit Veṇugrāma ('bamboo village'), the capital of the Rattas from the late 12th to early 13th century CE.

b_keladi.first_mention_attestation: First emerges in historical records around 1500 CE as the original seat of the Nayakas of Keladi under Chaudappa Nayaka, a feudatory of the Vijayanagara Empire.

morphemes.translation: settlement name (temple town in Shimoga district)

b_keladi.etymology_analysis: Kannada toponym of the Malnad temple town that served from c. 1500 CE as the first capital of the Keladi Nayaka dynasty.

b_gimhathiththa.first_mention_attestation: 14th-century CE Sri Lankan chronicles (Rajavaliya, Nikaya Sangrahaya) and Kelani/Alagakkonara epigraphs alongside Ibn Battuta's 1344 CE account documenting the rise of the Alagakkonara stronghold at Rayigama (Raigampura).
b_gimhathiththa.etymology_analysis: Sinhala contraction of 'Rājagrāma' ('royal village'), naming the medieval stronghold in Kalutara district that served as the seat of the Alagakkonara rulers and the 16th-century Kingdom of Raigama.

b_sitawaka.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 1521 CE, when Mayadunne established the Kingdom of Sitawaka following the partition of the Kingdom of Kotte (the Spoiling of Vijayabahu).

morphemes.translation: Sita (associated in local tradition with the Ramayana)

b_sitawaka.etymology_analysis: Sinhala Sītāvaka (modern Avissawella), a 16th-century CE royal capital founded in 1521 CE in south-central Sri Lanka.

b_kotte.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Pali chronicle Mahavamsa (c. 5th-6th century CE) as Kalyāṇī, the capital of provincial king Kelani Tissa and site of a major Buddhist vihara.

morphemes.translation: auspicious / beautiful (ancient city and temple name)

b_kotte.etymology_analysis: Sinhala Kelaniya derives from Pali/Sanskrit Kalyāṇī ('auspicious, beautiful'), an ancient Buddhist center on the Kelani River attested in the Mahavamsa.

b_dambadeniya.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Culavamsa (e.g., 12th-century CE campaigns of Parakramabahu I, c. 1140-1153 CE) as Vāpinagara in Dakkhinadesa.
b_dambadeniya.etymology_analysis: Pali Vāpinagara ('tank-city / reservoir-town'), recorded in the Culavamsa for 12th-century CE events in Dakkhinadesa.

b_malaya_rata.first_mention_attestation: Mahavamsa (c. 5th century CE Pali chronicle, Chapter 1) naming the sacred mountain Samantakuta (Sumanakuta), also attested in the 6th-century CE Tamil epic Manimekalai.
b_malaya_rata.etymology_analysis: Pali and Sanskrit oronym 'Samanta-kūṭa' ('Peak of Sumana/Saman'), the classical name of Adam's Peak (Samanala Kanda / Sri Pada) in the central highlands of Sri Lanka.

b_senkadagalapura.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the mid-14th century CE during the reign of Vikramabahu III (1357-1374 CE) as Senkadagalapura (modern Kandy).
b_senkadagalapura.etymology_analysis: Sinhala Seṅkaḍagalapura ('city of Senkadagala'), the 14th-century CE royal capital of Kandy, variously explained in folklore after a brahmin named Senkanda, a queen Senkanda, or a colored stone.

b_matale.first_mention_attestation: While nearby Aluvihara is attested in the Mahavamsa for the 1st-century BCE writing of the Pali Canon, the modern town name Matale (from Mahatala) lacks a confirmed contemporary pre-867 CE attestation.
b_matale.etymology_analysis: Sinhala Mātale is traditionally derived from Mahātala ('great plain/valley'), referring to its valley setting in central Sri Lanka.

b_batticaloa.first_mention_attestation: Early 17th-century CE European maritime accounts beginning with Dutch explorer Joris van Spilbergen's landing at Batticaloa (Matecalou / Batecaloa) in 1602 CE and the Portuguese fort built in 1628 CE, adapting the local Tamil name Mattakkalappu.
b_batticaloa.etymology_analysis: European colonial adaptation of Tamil 'Mattakkalappu' ('flat/muddy lagoon', Sinhala 'Madakalapuwa'), referring to the coastal lagoon city in eastern Sri Lanka.

b_dighavapi.first_mention_attestation: Dipavamsa (c. 4th century CE) and Mahavamsa (c. 5th century CE), attesting Dighavapi as a major ancient Buddhist stupa, reservoir, and settlement in eastern Sri Lanka.
b_dighavapi.etymology_analysis: Pali compound 'Dīgha-vāpī' ('long reservoir'), naming the ancient Buddhist pilgrimage site and irrigation settlement in Ampara district, eastern Sri Lanka.

b_mahiyangana.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Dipavamsa (c. 4th century CE) and Mahavamsa (c. 5th-6th century CE) as Mahiyangaṇa, site of an ancient Buddhist stupa in eastern Sri Lanka.
b_mahiyangana.etymology_analysis: Pali Mahiyangaṇa ('flat land / open ground', corresponding to Sinhala Bintenna), an ancient Buddhist shrine site recorded in the Pali chronicles.

b_magampura.first_mention_attestation: Mahavamsa (c. 5th century CE Pali chronicle, Chapter 22) recording Mahagama (Magama / Magampura) as the royal capital of the southern Rohana kingdom founded by Prince Mahanaga, corroborated by early Brahmi inscriptions in the Tissamaharama-Magama area.
b_magampura.etymology_analysis: Sinhala 'Magampura' derives from Pali 'Mahāgāma' ('great village/settlement') plus '-pura' ('city'), the ancient capital of Ruhuna in southern Sri Lanka.

b_katargama.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Mahavamsa (c. 5th-6th century CE) as Kājaragāma, whose kshatriya nobles attended the Bodhi Tree festival in the 3rd century BCE; Kiri Vehera stupa is dated archaeologically to the 1st century BCE.

morphemes.translation: desert / dry scrubland (or shortened from Kārttikeya)

b_katargama.etymology_analysis: Pali Kājaragāma (modern Kataragama) means either 'village in the dry/desert tract' (Sinhala katara-gama) or a contracted form of Kārttikeyagrāma.

b_godawaya.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Dipavamsa (c. 4th century CE) and Mahavamsa (c. 5th-6th century CE) as Mahāgāma (modern Tissamaharama), the ancient capital of Rohana.
b_godawaya.etymology_analysis: Pali Mahāgāma ('Great Village/Settlement') was the royal capital of the southern principality of Rohana from the 3rd-2nd century BCE.

b_jaffna.first_mention_attestation: Late 13th to 14th-century CE medieval Sri Lankan records (Culavamsa and Jaffna Kingdom chronicles) attesting Yapapatuna / Yapane and Tamil Yazhppanam as the northern port city of the Aryacakravarti rulers.
b_jaffna.etymology_analysis: Anglicized from Tamil 'Yazhppanam' (historically linked to medieval Sinhala 'Yapapatuna' / 'Yapane', 'port of Yapa', folk-etymologized in Tamil as the settlement of a blind harpist, 'yazh-panan').

historical_names.name: Nagadipa
historical_names.source: Vallipuram Gold Plate inscription of King Vasabha (c. 2nd century CE), Claudius Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE, Nagadiboi), and Mahavamsa (c. 5th century CE)
historical_names.notes: The Jaffna peninsula was known in antiquity as Nagadipa (Nakadiva in the 2nd-century CE Vallipuram inscription and Nagadiboi in Ptolemy) prior to the medieval emergence of Yapapatuna / Yazhppanam (Jaffna).

historical_names.name: Nakadiva
historical_names.source: Vallipuram Gold Plate inscription of King Vasabha (c. 2nd century CE), Claudius Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE, Nagadiboi), and Mahavamsa (c. 5th century CE)
historical_names.notes: The Jaffna peninsula was known in antiquity as Nagadipa (Nakadiva in the 2nd-century CE Vallipuram inscription and Nagadiboi in Ptolemy) prior to the medieval emergence of Yapapatuna / Yazhppanam (Jaffna).

b_mullaitivu.first_mention_attestation: No confirmed contemporary pre-867 CE attestation; villages in the Mullaitivu area appear in later medieval Sinhalese/Tamil works such as the 14th-15th century CE Nampota and Vanni chieftaincy records.
b_mullaitivu.etymology_analysis: Tamil Mullaittīvu combines mullai ('wild jasmine / forest tract') and tīvu ('island'), referring to the coastal lagoon settlement in northeastern Sri Lanka.

b_puttalam.first_mention_attestation: Ibn Battuta's Rihla (1344 CE), recording the fortified northwestern Sri Lankan port town of Pattala (identified with Puttalam) under the Aryacakravarti rulers.
b_puttalam.etymology_analysis: Commonly derived from Tamil 'uppu-talam' ('salt place/area', referring to the extensive coastal salt pans, contracted to Puttalam), or alternatively connected to 'pattinam' (port town).

b_mannar.first_mention_attestation: No confirmed pre-867 CE attestation of the Tamil name Maṉṉār; the nearby ancient port on the mainland was attested as Mahātittha in the Mahavamsa.
b_mannar.etymology_analysis: Tamil Maṉṉār means 'the raised place of sand', describing the sandy island off northwestern Sri Lanka.

historical_names.name: Mahatittha
historical_names.source: Mahavamsa (c. 5th-6th century CE)
historical_names.notes: Adjacent mainland port of Mahātittha (modern Mantai/Manthota) served as Anuradhapura's chief northwestern harbor.

b_kurunagala.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Mahavamsa (c. 5th-6th century CE) as Mahātittha (Tamil Māntoṭṭam / modern Mantai), the principal ancient maritime port of the Anuradhapura Kingdom.
b_kurunagala.etymology_analysis: Pali Mahātittha ('Great Port / Great Landing-place') was Sri Lanka's foremost ancient Indian Ocean emporium on the northwestern coast.

b_anuradhapura.first_mention_attestation: Claudius Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE, naming the inland royal city Anourogrammon), corroborated by the Dipavamsa (4th century CE), Mahavamsa (5th century CE), and early Brahmi inscriptions from the 3rd century BCE onward.
b_anuradhapura.etymology_analysis: Pali and Sanskrit 'Anurādha-pura' ('City of Anuradha', elevated from earlier Anuradhagama), the renowned ancient capital of Sri Lanka for over a millennium.

b_vavuniya.first_mention_attestation: No confirmed contemporary pre-867 CE attestation of the name Vavuniya; the forested borderland was historically part of the Vanni region.

morphemes.translation: toponym associated with Vanni / reservoir settlement

b_vavuniya.etymology_analysis: Modern Tamil Vavuṉiyā / Sinhala Vavuniyāva; earlier known as Vanni due to the abundance of Vanni trees in the northern forest belt.

b_dhamballai.first_mention_attestation: While cave occupation at the site has 1st-century BCE Brahmi inscriptions, the name Dambulla / Tampullai (Dhamballai) is attested in 12th-century CE inscriptions, notably the 1190 CE rock inscription of Nissanka Malla and a 12th-century CE Tamil inscription at Viharehinna.
b_dhamballai.etymology_analysis: Dhamballai reflects the medieval Tamil/Sinhalese form of Dambulla (Tamil Tampuḷḷai), a major cave-temple complex in central Sri Lanka.

historical_names.name: Jambukola Vihara
historical_names.source: Mahavamsa (c. 5th century CE Pali chronicle) and 1st-century BCE Brahmi cave inscriptions at the site
historical_names.notes: Associated in Pali chronicle tradition with Jambukola Vihara prior to the medieval Dambulla / Tampullai (Dhamballai) name (1190 CE).

b_polonnaruwa.first_mention_attestation: Culavamsa chronicle recording Pulatthinagara (Pulastipura, modern Polonnaruwa) as a royal seat from the 7th century CE onward, starting with King Aggabodhi III (r. 632–643 CE) and Aggabodhi IV (r. 667–683 CE).
b_polonnaruwa.etymology_analysis: Sinhala phonetic evolution of Pali 'Pulatthinagara' (Sanskrit 'Pulastipura', 'City of Pulastya'), an Anuradhapura-era royal residence that became Sri Lanka's medieval imperial capital.

b_trincomalee.first_mention_attestation: 7th-century CE Tamil Tevaram hymns composed by Shaiva saint Tirugnana Sambandar praising the shrine of Tirukonamalai (Konamamalai), of which Trincomalee is the anglicized form.
b_trincomalee.etymology_analysis: Colonial anglicization of Tamil 'Tirukonamalai' ('sacred hill of the Lord', referencing the Koneswaram promontory), which succeeded the older Sanskrit/Pali harbor name Gokarna/Gokanna.

historical_names.name: Gokarna
historical_names.source: Vayu Purana (c. 300 CE) as Gokarna and Mahavamsa (c. 5th century CE) as Gokanna
historical_names.notes: Prior to the 7th-century CE Tamil name Tirukonamalai, the harbor and temple site was attested in Sanskrit Puranas and Pali chronicles as Gokarna / Gokanna ('cow's ear').

historical_names.name: Gokanna
historical_names.source: Vayu Purana (c. 300 CE) as Gokarna and Mahavamsa (c. 5th century CE) as Gokanna
historical_names.notes: Prior to the 7th-century CE Tamil name Tirukonamalai, the harbor and temple site was attested in Sanskrit Puranas and Pali chronicles as Gokarna / Gokanna ('cow's ear').

b_devagiri.first_mention_attestation: Founded or established as a royal capital c. 1187 CE by Seuna (Yadava) king Bhillama V under the name Devagiri (later renamed Daulatabad in 1328 CE).
b_devagiri.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Devagiri ('Hill of the Gods') was the fortified citadel and capital of the Seuna (Yadava) dynasty from c. 1187 CE.

b_elapura.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Rashtrakuta Cave 15 inscription of Dantidurga (c. 753-757 CE) and the 812 CE Baroda copper-plate inscription, which explicitly names Elāpura (Ellora) as the site of Krishnaraja's Kailasa temple.
b_elapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Elāpura (modern Ellora / Verul) is the Rashtrakuta-era epigraphic name of the rock-cut cave and temple complex.

b_jhodga.first_mention_attestation: No confirmed contemporary pre-867 CE attestation; known for its medieval Hemadpanthi-style Manakeshvara/Mahadeo temple (c. 11th-13th century CE).
b_jhodga.etymology_analysis: Marathi village name (also spelled Zodga) in Malegaon taluka, Nashik district, famous for its medieval Hemadpanthi Shiva temple.

b_jalna.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested in the 16th century CE under the Ahmadnagar Sultanate (formerly Jalnapur, where governor Jamshid Khan built the Kali Masjid and reservoir c. 1557 CE).
b_jalna.etymology_analysis: Marathi toponym (earlier Jalnapur), rising to historical prominence in the 16th century CE under the Ahmadnagar Sultanate.

b_pratishthana.first_mention_attestation: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (c. 1st century CE, recording Paethana) and Claudius Ptolemy's Geography (c. 140 CE, naming Baithana as the royal capital of Satavahana king Sri Pulumavi), with the regional demonym Petenikas already in Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts (c. 250 BCE).
b_pratishthana.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit 'pratiṣṭhāna' ('firm foundation' or 'established seat', Prakrit Paithana, modern Paithan), the ancient capital of the Satavahana dynasty on the Godavari River in Maharashtra.

b_sindkhed.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested in 1450 CE when the Bahmani Sultan Alauddin Ahmad Shah granted the area as a jagir to a local Qazi.
b_sindkhed.etymology_analysis: Marathi Sindkheḍ (modern Sindkhed Raja), traditionally explained from Siddhakṣetra ('holy land of seers') or a legendary king Sindhurama, combining with Marathi kheḍ ('village').

b_bhainsa.first_mention_attestation: No confirmed contemporary pre-867 CE attestation of the name Bhainsa; local medieval tradition associates the site with Mahisha / Gopalji temple remains.
b_bhainsa.etymology_analysis: Indo-Aryan bhainsā ('buffalo', corresponding to Sanskrit Mahiṣa), a town in Nirmal district, Telangana, near the Maharashtra border.

b_vatsagulma.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 4th century CE as the capital of the Vatsagulma branch of the Vakataka dynasty founded by Sarvasena (c. 330-355 CE) and named in Vakataka inscriptions such as the Hisse-Borala and Washim copper plates.
b_vatsagulma.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Vatsagulma (modern Washim in Vidarbha, Maharashtra) was the royal capital of the Vatsagulma Vakatakas from the 4th century CE.

b_parnakheta.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Seuna (Yadava) records of the mid-12th century CE, recording that Mallugi (r. c. 1145-1160 CE) captured Parṇakheṭa (modern Patkhed in Akola district).
b_parnakheta.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Parṇakheṭa ('leaf-village / settlement of palasha trees'), identified with modern Patkhed in Akola district, Maharashtra.

b_mekhar.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested in the late 16th-century CE Ain-i-Akbari (c. 1590 CE) as the headquarters of a Mughal sarkar, though medieval Hemadpanthi remains exist locally.
b_mekhar.etymology_analysis: Marathi Mehkar (Mekhar) in Buldhana district, traditionally associated in local legend with the demon Meghankara.

b_hinawr.first_mention_attestation: Panjim copper-plate grant of Goa Kadamba King Jayakeshi I dated 1059 CE, explicitly naming Gopakapattana (modern Goa Velha) as the maritime capital of the Kadambas of Goa.
b_hinawr.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound 'Gopaka-pattana' ('port city of Gopaka/Goa'), the medieval Shilahara and Goa Kadamba emporium on the Zuari River in Goa.

b_honnore.first_mention_attestation: First famously documented in 1342 CE by the Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta as Hinawr (Honavar / Onore), ruled by Sultan Jamaluddin.
b_honnore.etymology_analysis: Honnore (modern Honnavar, Arabic Hinawr, Portuguese Onore) derives from Kannada Honnavara / Honnu-ūru ('golden town'), a major medieval coastal port on the Sharavati estuary.

b_gopakapattana.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested in the 17th century CE, notably when the Dutch East India Company established a trading factory (wakhar) at Vengurla in 1665 CE.
b_gopakapattana.etymology_analysis: Vengurla is a coastal port in Sindhudurg district, Maharashtra, explained in local Sateri temple tradition from veng ('mound') + urlā ('remained').

b_thana.first_mention_attestation: Al-Baladhuri's Kitab Futuh al-Buldan recording the 636 CE Arab naval expedition under Uthman ibn Abi al-As against the Konkan port of Tana (Thana), later attested as Sri-Sthanaka in 10th–11th century CE Shilahara copper-plate charters.
b_thana.etymology_analysis: Prakrit/Marathi evolution of Sanskrit 'Sthānaka' ('station' or 'administrative seat', modern Thane), the coastal capital of the North Konkan Shilaharas.

b_suraparaka.first_mention_attestation: No confirmed contemporary pre-867 CE attestation of the town name Dahanu; the nearby Mahalakshmi temple was built in 1306 CE by Jawhar ruler Jayaba Mukne.

morphemes.translation: coastal town and river name in Palghar district

b_suraparaka.etymology_analysis: Marathi coastal toponym Dāhāṇū in the northern Konkan (Palghar district, Maharashtra).

b_ambaranatha.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 1060 CE stone inscription at the Ambarnath Shiv Mandir built under the North Konkan Shilahara dynasty (Chhittaraja / Mummuni).
b_ambaranatha.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Ambaranātha ('Lord of the Sky', referring to Shiva in the open-roofed sanctum of the 1060 CE Shilahara temple).

b_chaul.first_mention_attestation: Attested by Pliny the Elder (c. 77 CE) as Symulla, Ptolemy (2nd century CE) as Timulla, and in 2nd-5th century CE Kanheri cave inscriptions in Prakrit as Chemulaka.
b_chaul.etymology_analysis: Marathi Chaul (from Prakrit Chemulaka / Chemuli, rendered in Greco-Roman sources as Symulla/Timulla) was a major Satavahana and Shilahara port at the mouth of the Kundalika River.

b_kondana.first_mention_attestation: First attested in historical chronicles in 1328 CE when Muhammad bin Tughluq captured the hill fortress of Kondhana from Koli chieftain Nag Naik (later renamed Sinhagad in 1670 CE).

morphemes.translation: fortress name associated with sage Kaundinya

b_kondana.etymology_analysis: Marathi Koṇḍhāṇā (Kondana), traditionally linked to the sage Kauṇḍinya; renamed Sinhagad ('Lion's Fort') by Shivaji in 1670 CE.

b_jirnanagara.first_mention_attestation: Earliest epigraphic attestation of the name (as Jimninagara / Jirnanagara) is in a 10th-century CE Sinda copper-plate grant (Saka 887 / 965 CE); 1st–3rd century CE Satavahana and Western Kshatrapa cave inscriptions at Junnar do not contain the name Jirnanagara or Junnar.
b_jirnanagara.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Jīrṇanagara ('Old City'), the reconstructed Sanskrit prototype of modern Junnar, an ancient Satavahana-era trade center on the Naneghat pass.

b_bhimashankara.first_mention_attestation: Attested in writings and temple construction dating back to the 13th century CE (c. 1201-1300 CE), when the black-stone Nagara/Hemadpanti Jyotirlinga shrine is documented.
b_bhimashankara.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Bhīmaśaṅkara ('Shiva of the Bhima / terrible Shiva'), a Jyotirlinga shrine at the source of the Bhima River in Pune district.

b_patkapur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE Maharashtra/Deccan historical sources (unoccupied holding slot in repository).
b_patkapur.etymology_analysis: Indo-Aryan -pur compound; unoccupied barony slot in the Kondana county with no confirmed pre-867 CE historical attestation in Maharashtra.

b_nasikya.first_mention_attestation: Katyayana's Varttika on Panini (c. 250 BCE) citing Nasikya as a city, preserved in Patanjali's Mahabhashya (c. 150 BCE), and extensively corroborated by 1st–2nd century CE Satavahana Brahmi inscriptions at the Pandavleni (Trirashmi) caves.
b_nasikya.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit 'Nāsikya' (modern Nashik), attested from 3rd-century BCE grammatical literature and Satavahana epigraphy; traditionally derived from Sanskrit 'nāsikā' (nose) via the Ramayana Panchavati episode.

b_seunapura.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the late 9th century CE (c. 880 CE) by Seunachandra I of the Seuna (Yadava) dynasty, who established Seunapura (identified with modern Sinnar).

eponym.details: Named after Seunachandra I (late 9th century CE, c. 870-900 CE), the second ruler of the Seuna (Yadava) dynasty who founded the town as his capital.

b_seunapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Seuṇapura ('City of Seuna'), founded by Seunachandra I in the late 9th century CE and identified with Sinnar in Nashik district.

b_ankai.first_mention_attestation: Constructed around 1000 years ago (c. 10th-11th century CE) by the Yadavas of Devagiri, with Jain caves at the base dated to the late Rashtrakuta/Yadava period.

morphemes.translation: hill fort name in the Satmala range

b_ankai.etymology_analysis: Marathi hill-fort toponym (Ankai-Tankai) in Yeola taluka, Nashik district, built by the Yadavas around the 10th-11th century CE.

b_ahmadnagar.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1494 CE by Malik Ahmad Nizam Shah I on the left bank of the Sina River as the capital of the newly independent Ahmadnagar Sultanate.

eponym.details: Named after Malik Ahmad Nizam Shah I (founder of the Nizam Shahi dynasty of the Ahmadnagar Sultanate), who established the city as his capital in 1494 CE.

morphemes.translation: Malik Ahmad Nizam Shah I (personal name)

b_ahmadnagar.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Persian-Indic eponymous compound 'Ahmad-nagar' ('City of Ahmad'), named directly after its 1494 CE founder Malik Ahmad Nizam Shah I.

b_lattalura.first_mention_attestation: Early 9th-century CE Rashtrakuta copper-plate charters and stone inscriptions under Govinda III and Amoghavarsha I styling the dynasty 'Lattalura-puravaradhishvara' ('Lord of Lattalura, the best of cities').
b_lattalura.etymology_analysis: Sanskritized Old Kannada toponym 'Lattalūra' (modern Latur in Maharashtra), attested in imperial Rashtrakuta charters as the ancestral seat of the dynasty.

b_nanded.first_mention_attestation: Attested in a Vakataka-era copper-plate inscription from Washim as Nanditaṭa (and also known as Nandigrāma), evolving into modern Nanded.
b_nanded.etymology_analysis: Marathi Nanded derives from Sanskrit Nanditaṭa ('bank of Nandi / Nanda', on the Godavari River), attested in the Washim copper-plate inscription.

b_bhid.first_mention_attestation: Early history is obscure; archaeological remains (such as the Kankaleshwar temple) suggest foundation during the Yadava period, likely under Singhana II (1210-1247 CE), with clear chronicle records by 1317-1341 CE.

morphemes.translation: town name (Beed, possibly from a low-lying / crowded basin)

b_bhid.etymology_analysis: Marathi Bīḍ (Beed, rendered Bhid in the repository), a medieval Marathwada town likely founded under the Yadavas of Devagiri in the 13th century CE.

b_darur.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 806 CE in a Rashtrakuta copper-plate inscription of Emperor Govinda III discovered at Dharur, Beed district.
b_darur.etymology_analysis: Dharur (also known as Kille Dharur) is attested in a Rashtrakuta copper-plate grant of Govinda III dated 806 CE. The toponym combines a local Indo-Aryan/Prakrit root dhar ('ridge/edge') with the Deccan town suffix -ur.

b_qandhar.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 10th century CE (c. 950 CE) when Rashtrakuta king Krishna III fortified Kandhar (also styled Krishnadurga).

morphemes.translation: fortified stronghold along the Manyad River

b_qandhar.etymology_analysis: Kandhar (rendered in the repository as Tschandhar) is historically associated with the 10th-century CE Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna III of Manyakheta, who constructed Kandhar Fort. No contemporary pre-867 CE written attestation of the name Kandhar is documented.

b_karahataka.first_mention_attestation: Attested c. 200 BCE in Brahmi/Prakrit votive inscriptions (mentioning donors from Karhakada) and early Buddhist cave records near Karad.
b_karahataka.etymology_analysis: Karahataka (Prakrit Karhakada, modern Karad) is one of the oldest epigraphically attested settlements in southern Maharashtra, appearing in inscriptions of c. 200 BCE. The name is traditionally derived from Sanskrit/Prakrit elements meaning 'elephant market'.

b_miraj.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1024 CE in the Miraj copper-plate inscription of Western Chalukya king Jayasimha II (Shaka 946), referring to the Mirinje division.

morphemes.translation: historic administrative division and fort town of Miraj

b_miraj.etymology_analysis: Miraj appears in 11th-century CE Western Chalukya and Kolhapur Shilahara epigraphs as Mirinje or Mairinja (notably the 1024 CE Miraj copper-plate grant of Jayasimha II). No contemporary written attestation exists prior to 867 CE.

b_karhada.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 6th–7th centuries CE in copper-plate charters (such as the Undikavatika grant) of the early Rashtrakuta ruler Abhimanyu of Manapura.
b_karhada.etymology_analysis: Manapura was the seat of an early Rashtrakuta lineage under King Abhimanyu in the 6th–7th centuries CE, identified by V. V. Mirashi with Man in Satara district. The name combines the regional name Mana with Sanskrit pura ('city').

b_pundarika.first_mention_attestation: First undisputed epigraphic attestation of Pandharpur (as Pandarage) is in a 1237 CE inscription; the Sanskritized form Paundarika Kshetra / Pundarika appears in medieval Varkari and copper-plate records.

morphemes.translation: white lotus (also linked to sage Pundalika)

b_pundarika.etymology_analysis: Pundarika (Paundarika Kshetra) is the Sanskritized sacred name of Pandharpur, associated with the devotee Pundalika and Sanskrit pundarika ('white lotus'). Because the identification of Pandharpur with the 516 CE Pandarangapalli grant is disputed and the first undisputed inscription dates to 1237 CE, it is not contemporarily attested by 867 CE.

b_kolhapur.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Kolhapur in 11th–12th century CE records, including the 1024 CE Miraj copper-plate of Jayasimha II and a 1126 CE Shilahara inscription of Gandaraditya I.
b_kolhapur.etymology_analysis: Kolhapur is attested under this name from the 11th century CE under the Western Chalukyas and Kolhapur Shilaharas (also appearing in Shilahara records as Kshullakapura and Kalapuri). Traditional etymology derives it from Kolhasura + pura ('city').

b_kurundaka.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 915 CE in the Bagumra copper-plate grant recording Rashtrakuta Emperor Indra III's coronation at Kurundaka on 24 February 915 CE.

morphemes.translation: amaranth / local plant or settlement root

b_kurundaka.etymology_analysis: Kurundaka (modern Kurundwad) is first documented in 915 CE as the site of Rashtrakuta Emperor Indra III's coronation. No pre-867 CE written attestation is recorded.

b_pranala.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1191–1192 CE in a Satara copper-plate inscription of Shilahara ruler Bhoja II referring to the hill fort of Pranalaka (Panhala).
b_pranala.etymology_analysis: Pranala (or Pranalaka, modern Panhala) is attested in 12th-century CE Shilahara inscriptions under Bhoja II (1191–1192 CE). There is no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_naldurg.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 16th century CE (c. 1558 CE) when the fort was rebuilt and named Naldurg under the Adil Shahi Sultanate of Bijapur.
b_naldurg.etymology_analysis: Naldurg (rendered as Naldurch) combines the traditional name Nal (Nalraja) with Sanskrit durga ('fortress'). While earlier fortifications existed, the name Naldurg is attested only in the medieval/early modern period.

b_sholapur.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1316 CE (Shaka 1238) in a Sanskrit inscription at Kamati in Mohol as Sonalipur (and in Solapur fort inscriptions as Sonalpur).
b_sholapur.etymology_analysis: Solapur (formerly Sholapur, rendered Scholapur) derives from earlier Kannada/Sanskrit forms Sonnalage / Sonalipur, attested in 12th–14th century CE Kalachuri and post-Yadava records (1316 CE). No pre-867 CE attestation exists.

b_purnagiri.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE Deccan records; associated in later medieval Tantric and Ain-i-Akbari (1596 CE) traditions with the Tulja Bhavani Shakti Peetha.
b_purnagiri.etymology_analysis: Purnagiri ('full mountain' in Sanskrit) appears as a Shakti Peetha designation in later Tantric texts, sometimes identified with Tuljapur in Dharashiv district. There is no contemporary pre-867 CE attestation for this site under the name Purnagiri.

b_ausa.first_mention_attestation: Ausa Fort was developed around c. 1200 CE, with its earliest surviving dated inscriptions belonging to the Nizam Shahi period (1529 CE).

morphemes.translation: historic fort town in Latur district

b_ausa.etymology_analysis: Ausa is a medieval fort town in Latur district whose fortification dates to c. 1200 CE. No pre-867 CE written attestation is documented.

b_taradavadi.first_mention_attestation: Attested in late 10th-century CE records (c. 973 CE) as Tardavadi-1000, the Rashtrakuta province governed by Tailapa II before he founded the Western Chalukya Empire.
b_taradavadi.etymology_analysis: Taradavadi (Tardavadi-1000 in Vijayapura/Bijapur district) was a key Rashtrakuta administrative province in the 10th century CE under Tailapa II. It is not attested in written sources prior to 867 CE.

b_hastikundi.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 893 CE in inscriptions of the Rashtrakutas of Hastikundi (Hathundi, 893–996 CE).
b_hastikundi.etymology_analysis: Hastikundi ('elephant pool' in Sanskrit) is historically attested from 893 CE as the seat of a Rashtrakuta branch (in Rajasthan, placed in Taradavadi in the repository). It is post-867 CE.

b_vijayapura_bis.first_mention_attestation: Attested in a Western Chalukya inscription of 1074–1075 CE as Vijayapura, founded by the Kalyani Chalukyas in the 10th–11th centuries CE.
b_vijayapura_bis.etymology_analysis: Vijayapura ('City of Victory' in Sanskrit, later Bijapur) was established by the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani in the 10th–11th centuries CE and is epigraphically attested by 1074–1075 CE.

b_acalapura.first_mention_attestation: Attested by the mid-8th century CE (c. 753 CE) in early Rashtrakuta records (Tivarkhed and Multhai plates) issued from Achalapura (modern Achalpur/Ellichpur).
b_acalapura.etymology_analysis: Achalapura (rendered Atschalapure, modern Achalpur) was the capital of an early Rashtrakuta branch in Berar/Vidarbha and is attested in pre-867 CE copper-plate grants (Tivarkhed, Multhai, and 753 CE Samangadh context).

b_amraoti.first_mention_attestation: Earliest concrete epigraphic attestation for the settlement (as Umbravati / Udumbravati -> Amravati) is the 1097 CE Adinath Jain statue inscription (prior to the 1722 CE Maratha grant to Ranoji Bhosle).
b_amraoti.etymology_analysis: Amravati (historically spelled Amraoti) is a later Sanskritization/corruption of the older name Udumbravati (Prakrit Umbravati, 'abounding in fig trees'), and is documented under the modern name from 1722 CE.

b_kalam.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1596–1597 CE in the Ain-i-Akbari as the headquarters of the Mughal Sarkar of Kalam in Berar Subah.
b_kalam.etymology_analysis: Kalam (modern Kalamb in Yavatmal district) is first prominently documented in the Ain-i-Akbari (1596–1597 CE) as a Mughal revenue sarkar; a 13th-century CE Harihara sculpture is also known from the town, but there is no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_wun.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE written sources under the name Wun (modern Wani, Yavatmal district).
b_wun.etymology_analysis: Wun is the colonial-era spelling of Wani in Yavatmal district. While the surrounding area has prehistoric and Satavahana-era archaeological remains, the settlement name Wun/Wani has no verified pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_gawilgarh.first_mention_attestation: Rebuilt and fortified in stone in 1425 CE by Bahmani Sultan Ahmad Shah I Wali while encamped at Ellichpur, as recorded in Firishta's chronicle.
b_gawilgarh.etymology_analysis: Compound 'Gawīl-gaṛh' ('Fort of the Gawlis'), referring to the earlier mud stronghold of the local Gawli pastoralists in the Melghat/Satpura hills before its 1425 CE Bahmani reconstruction.

b_canda.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the late 15th century CE (c. 1470–1495 CE) when Gond king Khandkya Ballal Shah founded Chanda (modern Chandrapur).
b_canda.etymology_analysis: Chanda (rendered Tschande, officially Chandrapur since 1964) was founded as a walled fort city by the Gond ruler Khandkya Ballal Shah in the late 15th century CE. No pre-867 CE attestation exists.

b_nagpur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested under the vernacular form Paunar/Panar before 867 CE; the site was known in the 5th century CE as Pravarapura.
b_nagpur.etymology_analysis: Panar/Paunar in Wardha district is the modern Marathi phonetic evolution of Pravarapura, the 5th-century CE Vakataka capital established under Pravarasena II (r. c. 420–455 CE). While Pravarapura is attested pre-867 CE, the vernacular form Panar/Paunar is post-867.

historical_names.name: Pravarapura
historical_names.source: Vakataka copper-plate charters of Pravarasena II (r. c. 420–455 CE)
historical_names.notes: Paunar is the later vernacular form of Vakataka Pravarapura.

b_bhandara.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1100 CE in a stone inscription at Ratanpur as Bhannara.
b_bhandara.etymology_analysis: Bhandara derives from Bhannara, first epigraphically attested in a stone inscription at Ratanpur dated 1100 CE. No pre-867 CE attestation is documented.

b_ramagiri.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the early 5th century CE in Vakataka inscriptions and Kalidasa's Meghaduta as Ramagiri (modern Ramtek Hill).
b_ramagiri.etymology_analysis: Ramagiri ('hill of Rama' in Sanskrit, modern Ramtek) served as the main religious sanctuary of the Vakataka dynasty from at least the early 5th century CE and is celebrated in classical Sanskrit literature.

b_kundina_SOUTHINDIA.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical Sanskrit epic literature (Mahabharata, c. 4th century BCE–4th century CE) as Kundinapuri, capital of Vidarbha (modern Kaundinyapura).

morphemes.translation: ancient Vidarbha capital associated with sage Kaundinya

b_kundina_SOUTHINDIA.etymology_analysis: Kundina (Kundinapuri, modern Kaundinyapura on the Purna River in Amravati district) is attested in classical Sanskrit epic tradition as the capital of ancient Vidarbha and is corroborated by Early Historic excavations.

b_kherla.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1398 CE in Indo-Persian chronicles as the capital of the Gond kingdom of Kherla under Narsingh Rai.
b_kherla.etymology_analysis: Kherla (in Betul district, Madhya Pradesh) was the seat of one of the four historical Gond kingdoms and is attested from the late 14th century CE (1398 CE) prior to its conquest by Hoshang Shah of Malwa in 1433 CE.

b_seoni.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1774 CE by Diwan Muhammad Amin Khan, who moved his administrative headquarters here from Chhapara.

morphemes.translation: settlement named after the seona (Gmelina arborea) tree

b_seoni.etymology_analysis: Seoni (rendered Sôni, formerly spelled Seeonee) was founded in 1774 CE by Diwan Muhammad Amin Khan. There is no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_vairagara.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the late 11th century CE in Tamil inscriptions of Chola emperor Kulottunga I (r. 1070–1122 CE) as Vayiragaram (modern Wairagarh).
b_vairagara.etymology_analysis: Vairagara (Wairagare, Tamil Vayiragaram, modern Wairagarh in Gadchiroli district) derives from Sanskrit Vajrakara/Vajragara ('diamond mine') and is first attested in 11th-century CE Chola inscriptions of Kulottunga I.

b_gondia.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 1888 CE with the opening of Gondia Railway Station (and municipal council in 1920 CE).
b_gondia.etymology_analysis: Gondia is a modern town in eastern Maharashtra named after the Gond inhabitants (or local gond/gum trade), emerging in the late 19th century CE around the 1888 CE railway junction.

b_panaji.first_mention_attestation: 1653 CE capture and renaming as Vijaydurg (Vijayadurga) by Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, expanding the older Shilahara coastal fort originally built by Raja Bhoja II (1193–1205 CE) as Gheria.
b_panaji.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound 'vijaya-durga' ('Fort of Victory'), bestowed by Shivaji in 1653 CE upon the coastal Konkan fortress previously known as Gheria in Sindhudurg district, Maharashtra.

b_dabhol.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the mid-14th century CE (after 1347 CE) as a major seaport of the Bahmani Sultanate in South Konkan.

morphemes.translation: coastal port town in Ratnagiri district

b_dabhol.etymology_analysis: Dabhol (medieval Mustafabad / Dabul) rose to prominence as a Bahmani and Adil Shahi port from the 14th century CE onward. No pre-867 CE written attestation of the name Dabhol exists.

b_chiplun.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 8th century CE during Badami Chalukya rule as Chiprarulana (modern Chiplun).
b_chiplun.etymology_analysis: Chiprarulana (rendered Tschiprarulana) is the 8th-century CE Chalukya-era form of Chiplun in Ratnagiri district, attested prior to 867 CE.

b_kollapura.first_mention_attestation: Attested in medieval Konkan/Shilahara and Yadava-era records (c. 11th–12th centuries CE) as Sangameshwar.

morphemes.translation: confluence (of the Shastri and Sonavi rivers)

b_kollapura.etymology_analysis: Sangamesvara (Sangameshwar in Ratnagiri district) means 'Lord of the Confluence' in Sanskrit, referring to the junction of the Shastri and Sonavi rivers. It is attested in medieval Konkan records after 867 CE.

b_kannanur.first_mention_attestation: Early 14th-century CE historical accounts by Persian chronicler Rashid al-Din (Jami' al-Tawarikh, c. 1300 CE) and Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta (c. 1342 CE) documenting the Kolathiri Malabar port of Kannanur (Kannur / Cannanore).
b_kannanur.etymology_analysis: Malayalam 'Kaṇṇan-ūr' ('place of Kannan/Krishna', also linked to early settlement Kanathur; anglicized as Cannanore), a major spice-trading port of the Kolathiri rulers in northern Kerala.

historical_names.name: Naura
historical_names.source: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st century CE)
historical_names.notes: Classical Greco-Roman trade accounts identify the early historic Malabar port of Naura (1st century CE) in the Kannur/Ezhimala coastal belt prior to the medieval emergence of Kannanur.

b_udayavara.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 13th century CE with the foundation of the Sri Krishna Matha by Madhvacharya (1238–1317 CE).
b_udayavara.etymology_analysis: Udupi is derived either from Tulu Odipu ('elevated land') or Sanskrit Udupa ('moon'). While nearby Udyavara was an Alupa capital, the town name Udupi is attested only from the medieval period (13th century CE).

historical_names.name: Udyavara
historical_names.source: 7th–8th century CE Old Kannada Alupa inscriptions at Udyavara
historical_names.notes: Nearby Udyavara (Udayapura) served as the Alupa capital from the 7th–8th centuries CE prior to the medieval rise of Udupi (1238 CE).

historical_names.name: Udayapura
historical_names.source: 7th–8th century CE Old Kannada Alupa inscriptions at Udyavara
historical_names.notes: Nearby Udyavara (Udayapura) served as the Alupa capital from the 7th–8th centuries CE prior to the medieval rise of Udupi (1238 CE).

b_mangalur.first_mention_attestation: Attested in a 7th-century CE copper-plate inscription of the Alupa dynasty as Mangalapura.
b_mangalur.etymology_analysis: Mangaluru (Mangalur / Mangalore) is attested in a 7th-century CE copper-plate inscription as Mangalapura (earlier also linked to Ptolemy's 2nd-century CE Maganoor). It combines Mangala ('auspicious' / Mangaladevi) with Dravidian uru ('town').

b_calicut.first_mention_attestation: Early 12th-century CE foundation of Kozhikode (Calicut) by the Eradi Zamorins following their conquest of Polanad (c. 1100–1124 CE), later recorded as Qaliqut in Ibn Battuta's 1342 CE Rihla.
b_calicut.etymology_analysis: Europeanized form (via Arabic Qaliqut) of Malayalam 'Kozhikode', widely derived from 'kōyil-kōṭṭa' ('fortified palace'), the seat of the Zamorins on the Malabar Coast.

b_malappuram.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources under the name Malappuram.
b_malappuram.etymology_analysis: Malappuram means 'land atop the hills' in Malayalam. While nearby Kurumathur has an 871 CE inscription, the town name Malappuram itself has no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_palakkad.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the modern period (Palakkad Fort built in 1766 CE by Hyder Ali); no pre-867 CE written attestation of the name Palakkad.
b_palakkad.etymology_analysis: Palakkad (Palghat) derives from Malayalam pala (Alstonia scholaris tree) + kadu ('forest'). Although the Palakkad Gap was a major ancient trade corridor, the settlement name Palakkad is post-867 CE.

b_mahoyadapuram.first_mention_attestation: Late 8th to early 9th-century CE Tamil Tevaram hymns of Sundarar referencing Makotai (Mahodayapuram), corroborated by 9th-century CE Chera Perumal inscriptions and Sankaranarayana's Laghubhaskariyavivarana (869 CE).
b_mahoyadapuram.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit 'Mahodayapuram' ('city of great prosperity', Tamil 'Makotai', modern Kodungallur), the royal capital of the medieval Chera Perumals of Kerala.

b_kunjakari.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical or epigraphic sources.
b_kunjakari.etymology_analysis: Kunjakari appears in the repository as a Kerala barony (used in-game as a Malabar Jewish site) without a verified historical settlement attestation in pre-modern records.

b_kottayam.first_mention_attestation: Attested from c. 1103 CE with the rise of the Thekkumkur kingdom following the partition of Vempolinad.
b_kottayam.etymology_analysis: Kottayam derives from Malayalam Kottaykkakam ('inside the fort', referring to Thaliyilkotta, the palace-fortress of the Thekkumkur rulers), emerging after Vempolinad split in 1103 CE.

b_mahal.first_mention_attestation: Ibn Battuta's Rihla (1343–1344 CE), recording the royal capital island of the Maldives as Mahal (Dhibat al-Mahal, modern Malé).
b_mahal.etymology_analysis: Medieval form of Malé, derived from Sanskrit 'mahā-ālaya' ('great house/palace', also assimilated to Arabic 'mahal'), attested as Dhibat al-Mahal in Ibn Battuta's 1343 CE account.

historical_names.name: Divi
historical_names.source: Ammianus Marcellinus (362 CE, Divi) and Sulaiman al-Tajir (851 CE, Dibajat)
historical_names.notes: Classical and 9th-century CE Arab sources attest the Maldivian archipelago as Divi (362 CE) and Dibajat (851 CE) prior to the appearance of Mahal / Dhibat al-Mahal in 1343 CE.

historical_names.name: Dibajat
historical_names.source: Ammianus Marcellinus (362 CE, Divi) and Sulaiman al-Tajir (851 CE, Dibajat)
historical_names.notes: Classical and 9th-century CE Arab sources attest the Maldivian archipelago as Divi (362 CE) and Dibajat (851 CE) prior to the appearance of Mahal / Dhibat al-Mahal in 1343 CE.

b_thiladhunmathi.first_mention_attestation: Attested in early 11th-century CE historical traditions regarding the Chola conquest of the northern Maldives under Rajaraja Chola I.
b_thiladhunmathi.etymology_analysis: Thiladhunmathi is the largest and northernmost atoll of the Maldives. Its earliest recorded political history in written accounts dates to the 11th-century CE Chola expeditions, with no pre-867 CE attestation.

b_kollam.first_mention_attestation: 825 CE inception of the Kollam Era (Kolla Varsham) and the 849 CE Tharisapalli (Quilon) Syrian copper plates issued by Venad ruler Ayyan Adikal Thiruvadikal under Chera monarch Sthanu Ravi Kulasekhara.
b_kollam.etymology_analysis: Malayalam toponym (Europeanized as Quilon) variously linked to Sanskrit 'kollam' (black pepper / ship harbor) or Malayalam 'koyil-illam' (royal palace homestead), a premier 9th-century Malabar maritime emporium.

b_vizhinjam.first_mention_attestation: Attested in late 8th-century CE Pandya inscriptions (under Maran Chadayan, r. 765–815 CE) as the port capital of the Ay/Vel ruler of Vizhinjam.

morphemes.translation: ancient Ay port and coastal fortress

b_vizhinjam.etymology_analysis: Vizhinjam (rendered Vidschinjam) served as the headquarters of the Ay dynasty in the 8th century CE and is attested in Pandya-Ay war inscriptions from the reign of Maran Chadayan (765–815 CE).

b_kottar.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 1st century CE by Pliny the Elder (23–79 CE) as Cottora and c. 130–150 CE by Ptolemy as Kottiara Metropolis.
b_kottar.etymology_analysis: Kottar (Kottaru, now part of Nagercoil) was an ancient Pandya-Chera mercantile emporium on the Pahrali River, attested by Pliny the Elder (1st century CE) and Ptolemy (2nd century CE).

b_tanjavur.first_mention_attestation: 8th-century CE Sendalai pillar inscriptions of Perumbidugu Mutharaiyar II styling the Mutharaiyars 'Tanjai-kon' ('Lords of Tanjai'), corroborated by early Tamil Bhakti literature and Vijayalaya Chola's mid-9th century capture.
b_tanjavur.etymology_analysis: Tamil 'Tañcai-ūr' (Thanjavur), traditionally derived from 'tañcam' ('refuge') plus 'ūr' ('town'), attested in 8th-century Mutharaiyar epigraphy before becoming the imperial Chola capital.

b_tirukoilur.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 7th–9th century CE Alvar hymns (Nalayira Divya Prabandam) and 7th-century CE temple foundations as Tirukkovilur (earlier Sangam Kovalur).
b_tirukoilur.etymology_analysis: Tirukoilur ('sacred temple town' in Tamil) evolved from the Sangam-period name Kovalur (seat of the Malayaman chiefs) and is attested in early medieval Alvar hymns by the 7th–9th centuries CE.

historical_names.name: Kovalur
historical_names.source: Sangam literature (c. 2nd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Originally known as Kovalur in the Sangam era before taking the prefix Tiru- ('sacred') and kovil ('temple').

historical_names.name: Koval
historical_names.source: Sangam literature (c. 2nd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Originally known as Kovalur in the Sangam era before taking the prefix Tiru- ('sacred') and kovil ('temple').

b_kannanur_2.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 13th century CE (c. 1228 CE) as Kannanur Koppam, the southern capital of the Hoysala Empire near Tiruchirappalli (modern Samayapuram).
b_kannanur_2.etymology_analysis: Kannanur (Kannanur Koppam, modern Samayapuram north of Tiruchirappalli) became prominent in the 13th–14th centuries CE as a Hoysala capital in Tamilakam. No pre-867 CE attestation is documented.

b_gangaikondacolapuram.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 1025 CE by Chola Emperor Rajendra Chola I to commemorate his northern Indian campaign to the Ganges, serving as the imperial Chola capital for roughly 250 years.

eponym.details: Named after Chola Emperor Rajendra Chola I (r. 1014–1044 CE), who assumed the title 'Gangaikonda Chola' ('the Chola who conquered the Ganges') after his northern expedition and founded the city c. 1025 CE.

b_gangaikondacolapuram.etymology_analysis: Tamil-Sanskrit royal title compound 'Gaṅgai-koṇṭa-Cōḻa-puram' ('City of the Chola who conquered the Ganges'), commemorating Rajendra Chola I's c. 1020–1025 CE Gangetic expedition.

b_nagapattinam.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 7th-century CE Tevaram hymns of Appar and Sambandar (as Nagai) and Pallava-era Buddhist vihara records under Narasimhavarman II (695–728 CE).
b_nagapattinam.etymology_analysis: Nagapattinam ('port town of the Nagar') is attested as Nagai in 7th-century CE Tevaram and Nalayira Divya Prabandam hymns, gaining the suffix -pattinam as a Chola maritime hub.

b_tagadur.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Sangam literature (Purananuru, c. 2nd century CE) as the capital of Athiyaman Neduman Anci (modern Dharmapuri).
b_tagadur.etymology_analysis: Tagadur (rendered Tagadûr, modern Dharmapuri) was the Sangam-era capital of the Athiyaman (Satyaputo) chieftains, celebrated in Purananuru verses by Avvaiyar.

b_kelrayan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary pre-867 CE written sources; later medieval traditions link the Kalrayan Hills jagirdars to the Vijayanagara period.
b_kelrayan.etymology_analysis: Kalrayan (Kalvarayan Hills, rendered Kelrayan) is a range in the Eastern Ghats of Tamil Nadu. No pre-867 CE written attestation of the name is documented.

b_srirangam.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the hymns of the Alvars (Nalayira Divya Prabandam, 6th–9th centuries CE), including Thondaradippodi Alvar and Thirumangai Alvar.
b_srirangam.etymology_analysis: Srirangam (Tamil Tiruvarangam) is the sacred Kaveri river island and Ranganathaswamy temple complex, glorified in Alvar Vaishnava poetry between the 6th and 9th centuries CE.

b_tiruvannamalai.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 7th century CE in the Tevaram hymns of Appar and Sambandar (and in the 9th-century CE Tiruvempavai of Manikkavacakar).
b_tiruvannamalai.etymology_analysis: Tiruvannamalai (rendered Tiruwannamalai) means 'sacred Annamalai' in Tamil, referring to the Arunachala hill and Shiva temple praised by 7th-century CE Nayanar saints Appar and Sambandar.

b_uttaramerur.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 8th century CE (c. 750 CE) in Pallava temple inscriptions under Nandivarman II and his successors.
b_uttaramerur.etymology_analysis: Uttaramerur (Uthiramerur) is attested in 8th-century CE Pallava inscriptions (around 25 Pallava records precede the famous 10th-century CE Chola village-assembly inscriptions of Parantaka I).

b_jinji.first_mention_attestation: 10th regnal year inscription of Chola king Vikrama Chola (c. 1128–1130 CE), where a Kadava feudatory calls himself Lord of Senjiyar of the strong embattled fort.
b_jinji.etymology_analysis: Gingee (Tamil: Senji, anglicized from Jinji/Senji) is linked in local tradition to the guardian goddess Senjiamman or to the Chola-era hill fortress. The earliest epigraphic attestation of the name Senjiyar dates to the 10th regnal year of Vikrama Chola (c. 1130 CE).

b_karavur.first_mention_attestation: Claudius Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) listing Karoura as the inland Chera royal capital, corroborated by classical Sangam Tamil literature and 1st–2nd century CE Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions at nearby Pugalur.
b_karavur.etymology_analysis: Old Tamil 'Karuvūr' / 'Karavūr' (modern Karur, Ptolemy's Karoura), the inland political capital (Vanci) of the Sangam-era Chera dynasty on the Amaravathi River in Tamil Nadu.
