b_tenkasi.first_mention_attestation: 15th-century CE inscriptions at the Kasi Viswanathar Temple in Tenkasi under Sadaiyavarman Parakrama Pandya (Tenkasi Pandyas, from 1422 CE).
b_tenkasi.etymology_analysis: Tenkasi combines Tamil 'ten' (south) with 'Kasi' (Varanasi), meaning 'Kashi of the South'. It was established as a temple capital in the 15th century CE by Parakrama Pandya.

b_kovai.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Chola-period and later Kongu Nadu traditions (post-10th century CE) associating Koyanputtur / Kovai with the chieftain Kovan or goddess Koniamman; the specific settlement name Kovai is not contemporarily attested by 867 CE.
b_kovai.etymology_analysis: Kovai is the shortened Tamil form of Koyamputtur (Coimbatore), derived from Kovanputtur ('new town of Kovan', an Irula chieftain) or from Koniamman/Kovaiamma, the local patron goddess.

b_tiruppur.first_mention_attestation: Chola-era Kongu Nadu epigraphy (10th–11th century CE) and local medieval records; the town name Tiruppur itself has no confirmed pre-867 CE attestation.
b_tiruppur.etymology_analysis: Tiruppur combines Tamil 'thiruppu' (to turn back) and 'ur' (place/town), traditionally explained as the place where cattle were turned back and restored to the Pandavas.

b_madurai.first_mention_attestation: Kautilya's Arthashastra and Megasthenes' Indica (c. 300 BCE), followed by 2nd-century BCE Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions at Mangulam and Sangam works such as Maturaikkanci.
b_madurai.etymology_analysis: Madurai (Old Tamil: Matirai / Maturai) is variously derived from Old Tamil 'matirai' (walled city) or Sanskrit 'Madhura' (sweetness), attested as the Pandyan capital from at least the 3rd–2nd century BCE.

b_tirunelveli.first_mention_attestation: 7th-century CE Tamil Shaiva canonical hymns of the Tevaram (Tirugnana Sambandar and Appar), which praise the shrine at Thirunelveli.
b_tirunelveli.etymology_analysis: Tirunelveli derives from Tamil 'thiru' (sacred), 'nel' (paddy), and 'veli' (hedge), referencing the Shaiva legend in which Shiva formed a protective hedge around a devotee's paddy crop.

b_rameshvaram.first_mention_attestation: Praised as Iramesuram (Rameswaram) in the 7th-century CE Tamil Tevaram hymns of Appar and Sambandar (c. 650 CE), with major temple sanctum reconstruction later under 12th-century CE Pandya and Sri Lankan rulers.
b_rameshvaram.etymology_analysis: Rameswaram (Sanskrit: Ramesvaram, from Rama + isvara) means 'Lord of Rama', referring to the Shiva lingam worshipped by Rama in Ramayana tradition; the surviving temple structure dates to the 12th century CE.

b_virudhukkalvetti.first_mention_attestation: 16th-century CE Madurai Nayak-period records (post-1559 CE) for Virudhukkalvetti (later renamed Virudhupatti in 1875 CE and Virudhunagar in 1923 CE).
b_virudhukkalvetti.etymology_analysis: Virudhukkalvetti (earlier name of Virudhunagar) comes from Tamil 'virudhu' (banner/trophy) and 'kalvetti' (cut/seized), commemorating a local resident who defeated a challenger and seized his banners.

b_sivakasi.first_mention_attestation: 15th-century CE foundation under Tenkasi Pandya king Arikesari Parakrama Pandya (r. 1428–1460 CE), who built the Viswanatha Swamy Temple.
b_sivakasi.etymology_analysis: Sivakasi ('Shiva's Kashi') was established in the early 15th century CE under Arikesari Parakrama Pandya around a lingam brought from Kashi (Varanasi).

b_korkai.first_mention_attestation: 1st-century CE Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (as Colchi), Ptolemy's Geographia (2nd century CE), and Sangam Tamil poetry (c. 1st–3rd century CE), corroborated by Tamil-Brahmi pottery (3rd century BCE–2nd century CE).
b_korkai.etymology_analysis: Korkai (Greek: Colchi / Kolkhoi) was the principal early historic port and pearl-fishery center of the Pandya kingdom at the mouth of the Thamirabarani River, attested from the 1st century CE.

b_kayal.first_mention_attestation: Marco Polo's travel account (visits in 1288 and 1293 CE), which describes Cail (Kayal) as the great port of the Later Pandya kingdom.
b_kayal.etymology_analysis: Kayal (modern Kayalpatnam) derives from Tamil 'kayal' (backwater or lagoon), referring to the coastal lagoon port that succeeded nearby Korkai as the main Pandyan emporium in the 13th century CE.

historical_names.name: Korkai
historical_names.source: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st century CE)
historical_names.notes: Korkai served as the earlier Pandyan port on the Thamirabarani delta before silting shifted maritime trade to Kayal.

b_uraiyur.first_mention_attestation: 1st-century CE Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (as Argaru) and Sangam literature (c. 1st–3rd century CE), where Uraiyur is the early Chola capital.
b_uraiyur.etymology_analysis: Uraiyur (Old Tamil: Uraiyur, 'dwelling town') was the inland capital of the early Cholas near Tiruchirappalli, attested in the 1st-century CE Periplus as Argaru and in Sangam literature.

b_dindigul.first_mention_attestation: 1538 CE Vijayanagara stone inscription of Emperor Achyuta Deva Raya at the Padmagirisvara temple atop Dindigul rock, preceding the construction of the Madurai Nayaka stone fort in 1605 CE.
b_dindigul.etymology_analysis: Anglicized from Tamil 'Tiṇṭukkal' ('pillow rock'), describing the massive rounded bare monolithic rock dominating the town and supporting Dindigul Fort in Tamil Nadu.

b_sivaganga.first_mention_attestation: 1730 CE foundation of the Sivaganga Kingdom by Raja Sasivarna Periya Oodaya Thevar.
b_sivaganga.etymology_analysis: Sivaganga ('Shiva's Ganges') was established in 1730 CE as the capital of the Sivaganga estate/kingdom by Sasivarna Thevar.

b_padaividu.first_mention_attestation: Early 11th-century CE foundation (c. 1000 CE) of Chandragiri Fort under Yadavaraya ruler Immadi Narasinga Yadavaraya, later attested in Vijayanagara epigraphy from 1367 CE onward.
b_padaividu.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound 'Candra-giri' ('Moon Hill'), naming the crescent-shaped hill fortress near Tirupati in Andhra Pradesh that served as the final Vijayanagara capital.

b_melpadi.first_mention_attestation: 959 CE Rashtrakuta campaign records of Krishna III (and Vemulavada Chalukya feudatory Vagaraja) and early Chola inscriptions at Melpadi, including Rajaraja I's Arinjisvara memorial shrine for Arinjaya Chola (d. c. 957 CE).
b_melpadi.etymology_analysis: Tamil compound 'mēl-pāṭi' ('western/upper encampment or settlement'), a strategic 10th-century Chola–Rashtrakuta frontier town in Vellore district, Tamil Nadu.

b_nangali.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-modern epigraphy by 867 CE; modern village in Mulbagal taluk, Kolar district, Karnataka, attested in colonial-era gazetteers and census records.

morphemes.translation: border village name of uncertain origin

b_nangali.etymology_analysis: Nangali is a border village in Mulbagal taluk, Kolar district, Karnataka; no pre-867 CE epigraphic attestation or established etymology is recorded.

b_muluvagil.first_mention_attestation: 11th-century CE Chola-era and subsequent Hoysala and Vijayanagara inscriptions from Kolar district (Epigraphia Carnatica Vol. X) attesting Mudalabagilu / Muluvagil (modern Mulbagal) as an eastern frontier gateway.
b_muluvagil.etymology_analysis: Contracted from Old Kannada 'Mūḍala-bāgilu' ('eastern gate/entrance', modern Mulbagal), marking the eastern pass of Kolar district toward Andhra and Tamil Nadu.

b_kuvalala.first_mention_attestation: 5th-century CE authentic Western Ganga copper-plate and stone inscriptions attesting Kuvalala (Kovalalapura, modern Kolar) as the earliest Western Ganga royal capital and basis of the imperial title Kovalalapura-paramesvara.
b_kuvalala.etymology_analysis: Early Sanskritized Kannada toponym 'Kuvalāla' (also Kolala / Kovalalapura, modern Kolar), the initial capital of the Western Ganga dynasty before their move to Talakadu.

b_kudalasangama_bis.first_mention_attestation: 12th-century CE temple inscriptions at Padavedu (Ammayappa Esvarar Temple) and 14th-century Sambuvaraya inscriptions (Sagaloga Chakravarthi Rajanarayana Sambuvarayar).
b_kudalasangama_bis.etymology_analysis: Padaividu (modern Padavedu) derives from Tamil 'padai' (army) and 'vidu' (camp/house), meaning 'military encampment', serving as the capital of the Sambuvarayar chiefs from the 13th–14th century CE.

b_nellore.first_mention_attestation: 13th-century CE inscriptions and records, when the city formerly known as Vikrama Simhapuri came to be called Nelluru (Nellore).
b_nellore.etymology_analysis: Nellore (Telugu: Nelluru, rendered 'Nellôr' in the repository) derives from 'nelli' (gooseberry/amla tree) or 'nellu' (paddy) plus 'uru' (town). It replaced the earlier medieval name Vikrama Simhapuri in the 13th century CE.

b_vallurapura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE epigraphy under the exact name Vallurapura; associated with the Telugu-region village name Valluru (Vallur) plus Sanskrit '-pura'.
b_vallurapura.etymology_analysis: Vallurapura is a Sanskritized form of Valluru/Vallur (a village name found in Nellore and Kadapa districts) with the suffix '-pura' (city/town).

b_kalahasti.first_mention_attestation: 7th-century CE Tamil Shaiva hymns of the Tevaram (Appar, Sundarar, and Sambandar), which classify the shrine at Kalahasti as a Paadal Petra Sthalam.
b_kalahasti.etymology_analysis: Kalahasti (Srikalahasti) derives from the Shaiva legend of three devotees of Shiva—a spider (sri), a serpent (kala), and an elephant (hasti)—and is revered in the 7th-century CE Tevaram.

b_potapi.first_mention_attestation: 9th-century CE Dalavaypuram copper plates of Pandya king Parantaka Viranarayana and Madras Museum plates of Pottapi Choda king Srikantha Chola.
b_potapi.etymology_analysis: Potapi (Pottapi) was the seat of the Pottapi Chodas, a branch of the Telugu Chodas attested from the 9th century CE in copper-plate charters.

b_penugonda.first_mention_attestation: March 25, 1354 CE Kannada-Sanskrit inscription on the north gate bastion of Penukonda Fort (reign of Bukka Raya I) recording the construction of the stone fortress under minister Anantarasa and Prince Virupanna I.
b_penugonda.etymology_analysis: Telugu compound 'penu-koṇḍa' ('big hill', Sanskritized as Ghanagiri), naming the major Vijayanagara hill fortress and post-1565 refuge capital in Anantapur/Sri Sathya Sai district, Andhra Pradesh.

b_mangalavada.first_mention_attestation: 12th-century CE Kalachuri of Kalyani records (Bijjala II, c. 1157 CE) naming Mangalavada (modern Mangalavedhe) as their feudatory capital.
b_mangalavada.etymology_analysis: Mangalavada (modern Mangalavedhe, also Magaliveda) combines 'mangala' (auspicious) and 'vada' (enclosure/settlement), serving as the 12th-century CE capital of the Southern Kalachuris.

b_nandi.first_mention_attestation: Early 9th-century CE inscriptions (c. 806 and 810 CE) of Nolamba-Pallava ruler Nolambadhiraja and Rashtrakuta Emperor Govinda III at Nandi (Nandagiri / Nandi Hills).
b_nandi.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit oronym 'Nanda-giri' ('Nandi Hill', modern Nandi Hills / Nandidurga in Chikkaballapur district, Karnataka), attested in early 9th-century CE Nolamba and Rashtrakuta inscriptions.

b_togarakunta.first_mention_attestation: Late 11th to early 12th-century CE Western Chalukya stone inscription of Tribhuvanamalladeva (Vikramaditya VI) and Kumara Tailapadeva at Togarakunta, recording grants to the Chandraprabha Jain basadi at Togarikunte.

morphemes.translation: red madder dye plant (Morinda tinctoria) / red ochre

b_togarakunta.etymology_analysis: Telugu compound 'togara-kuṇṭa' ('pond of the red-dye plant / red soil', attested in Chalukya epigraphy as Togarikunte), a historic village in Anantapur/Rayalaseema, Andhra Pradesh.

b_anantapur.first_mention_attestation: 14th-century CE Vijayanagara-period tradition and records linking Anantasagaram/Anantapur to Chikka Vodeya, minister of Bukka Raya I (r. 1356–1377 CE).
b_anantapur.etymology_analysis: Anantapur (Ananthapuramu) derives from Anantasagaram ('endless ocean' tank) and '-pur' (city), founded in the 14th century CE during the Vijayanagara period.

b_puspagiri.first_mention_attestation: Surviving stone inscriptions at the Pushpagiri Temple Complex begin in the late 10th century CE (e.g., 991 CE inscription of Trailokya Malla Raju); earlier 7th-century CE dating rests on stylistic/traditional antiquity without a contemporary pre-867 CE epigraph naming Pushpagiri.
b_puspagiri.etymology_analysis: Pushpagiri ('flower hill') is a historic temple and educational center on the Penna River in Kadapa district, dating back to c. the 7th century CE.

b_kanchipuram.first_mention_attestation: Patanjali's Mahabhashya (c. 2nd century BCE) as Kanchipuraka, and 3rd–4th century CE Pallava inscriptions and Gupta Allahabad Pillar inscription as Kanchipura.
b_kanchipuram.etymology_analysis: Kanchipuram (rendered 'Kantschipuram' in the repository) combines 'Kanchi' (girdle, or linked to Brahma's worship) with 'puram' (city), serving as the Pallava capital and attested from the 2nd century BCE.

b_takkaloma.first_mention_attestation: 7th-century CE Tamil Shaiva hymns of the Tevaram (Jalantheeswarar Temple, a Paadal Petra Sthalam), later famous for the 949 CE Battle of Takkolam.
b_takkaloma.etymology_analysis: Takkolam (Thakkolam, rendered 'Takkaloma' in the repository) is a historic temple town in Tondaimandalam praised in the 7th-century CE Tevaram and the site of the 949 CE Chola-Rashtrakuta battle.

b_mamallapuram.first_mention_attestation: 7th-century CE Pallava inscriptions of Narasimhavarman I ('Mamalla', r. 630–670 CE), who founded/named the port city Mamallapuram.
b_mamallapuram.etymology_analysis: Mamallapuram ('city of Mamalla') is named after the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I (630–670 CE), titled Mamalla ('great wrestler').

b_pannagallu.first_mention_attestation: Mid-11th-century CE Kalyani Chalukya and Kunduru Choda inscriptions at Panagal (Nalgonda district) referring to the town as Panugallu.
b_pannagallu.etymology_analysis: Pannagallu (Panagal / Panugallu) is a historic Telangana temple town in Nalgonda district, attested in Kalyani Chalukya and Kunduru Choda inscriptions from the 11th century CE.

b_yetagiri.first_mention_attestation: 11th-century CE Chola (Rajadhiraja I, c. 1044–1053 CE) and Western Chalukya inscriptions mentioning Yetagiri (modern Yadgir).
b_yetagiri.etymology_analysis: Yetagiri (modern Yadgir / Yadavagiri) derives from 'Yadava' (the Seuna Yadava rulers) and 'giri' (hill), attested in 10th–11th century CE Western Chalukya and Chola records.

b_devarakonda.first_mention_attestation: 14th-century CE Recherla Padmanayaka Velama records (c. 1360 CE) when Madanayaka ruled Devarakonda alongside Rachakonda.
b_devarakonda.etymology_analysis: Devarakonda ('hill of the gods' in Telugu) was fortified as a major stronghold of the Recherla Nayakas (Velamas) in the 14th century CE.

b_racakonda.first_mention_attestation: Mid-14th century CE inscriptions (c. 1363–1369 CE) of Recherla Padmanayaka ruler Anapota Nayaka documenting the founding and fortification of Rachakonda as the Recherla capital.
b_racakonda.etymology_analysis: Telugu compound 'rāca-koṇḍa' ('royal hill'), naming the 14th-century cyclopean hill fortress established by the Recherla Nayakas in Yadadri Bhuvanagiri district, Telangana.

b_golkonda.first_mention_attestation: 1143 CE Kakatiya-era origin of the hilltop mud fort (Golla Konda) under the Kakatiya dynasty.
b_golkonda.etymology_analysis: Golkonda (Golconda) derives from Telugu 'Golla konda' ('shepherd's hill'), referring to the Kakatiya-era fortress founded c. 1143 CE and later expanded by the Qutb Shahis.

b_nalgonda.first_mention_attestation: 14th-century CE Bahmani-period records documenting the renaming of the medieval hill town of Nilagiri as Nalgunda (later Nalgonda).
b_nalgonda.etymology_analysis: Telugu compound 'nalla-koṇḍa' ('black hill'), evolving via medieval Bahmani-era Nalgunda from the earlier hill-town designation Nilagiri ('blue hill') in Telangana.

b_vemulavada.first_mention_attestation: 8th-century CE Vemulavada Chalukya inscriptions (c. 750 CE onward), which refer to their capital as Lembulapataka / Lemulavada.
b_vemulavada.etymology_analysis: Vemulawada (rendered 'Wemulawâde' in the repository; attested in Chalukya inscriptions as Lembulapataka / Lemulavada) served as the capital of the Chalukyas of Vemulavada from the 8th century CE.

b_balkonda.first_mention_attestation: March 28, 1242 CE Telugu Kakatiya stone inscription of Emperor Ganapatideva on a Nandi pedestal recording a land grant of 100 marttars in the village of Balakonda.
b_balkonda.etymology_analysis: Telugu hill-fort toponym 'Balakonda' (contracted to Balkonda), attested in 13th-century Kakatiya epigraphy and 15th-century Bahmani chronicles in Nizamabad district, Telangana.

b_indur.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Rashtrakuta-period fort and regional records of Indur (Indrapuri, later renamed Nizamabad).
b_indur.etymology_analysis: Indur (modern Nizamabad) is traditionally linked to Indrapuri / King Indradatta and Telugu 'ur' (town), with the Nizamabad hillfort dating to the 10th-century CE Rashtrakuta period.

b_ellur.first_mention_attestation: Earliest surviving inscription explicitly naming Mudigonda is the Saka 921 (999 CE) Mudigonda stone inscription (while the Koravi stone inscription of c. 892–921 CE under Eastern Chalukya Bhima I documents early Mudigonda Chalukya chief Kusumayudha I / Gonangayya); secondary c. 845 CE estimates lack contemporary <= 867 CE epigraphic attestation.
b_ellur.etymology_analysis: Mudigonda (rendered 'Mudigonde' in the repository) was the initial capital of the Mudigonda Chalukyas in Khammam district, active from c. 845 CE.

b_kambampet.first_mention_attestation: 14th-century CE late/post-Kakatiya Telugu inscriptions in the Khammam region and the Khammam Fort gateway epigraph attesting Khammamettu / Kambhammettu around the Stambhadri rock hill.
b_kambampet.etymology_analysis: Historic variant of Khammammett / Kambhammettu (modern Khammam), combining Telugu 'kambam' (from Sanskrit 'stambha', referring to the pillar-like Narasimha hill Stambhadri) with '-mettu' (elevation) / '-peta' (town).

b_vinukonda.first_mention_attestation: Kakatiya-period epigraphy (13th century CE) and 14th-century Reddi Kingdom records listing Vinukonda among the major hill forts of Palnadu.

morphemes.translation: to hear (legend of Rama hearing news)

b_vinukonda.etymology_analysis: Vinukonda ('hill of hearing' in Telugu) is a medieval hillfort in Guntur/Palnadu district attested in Kakatiya and Reddi-period inscriptions.

b_palwancha.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE epigraphy; modern village in Telangana (Katkuru).
b_palwancha.etymology_analysis: Katukuru (Katkuru) is a Telugu village name ending in '-uru' (settlement); no pre-867 CE epigraphic attestation is documented.

b_palampet.first_mention_attestation: 1213 CE Ramappa (Rudreshwara) Temple inscription at Palampet, recording its construction under Kakatiya general Recherla Rudra during Ganapati Deva's reign.
b_palampet.etymology_analysis: Palampet combines a local root with Telugu 'pet' (quarter/town) and is famously attested in the 1213 CE Kakatiya inscription of the Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple.

b_bhadracala.first_mention_attestation: 17th-century CE construction of the Bhadrachalam Rama Temple by Kancherla Gopanna (Bhadrachala Ramadasu).
b_bhadracala.etymology_analysis: Bhadrachalam ('Bhadra's hill') is named after the mythological sage Bhadra and rose to prominence in the 17th century CE with the construction of its Rama temple by Kancherla Gopanna.

b_mancherial.first_mention_attestation: 9th-century CE Gond tradition attributing Sirpur Fort to Gond ruler Bhim Ballal Singh (though historical Chanda Gond consolidation is often dated later, c. 1320 CE).
b_mancherial.etymology_analysis: Sirpur (Sirpur-Tandur, formerly Suryapuram) combines 'Sir' (from Sri/Surya) and '-pur' (city). While local tradition attributes Sirpur Fort to the 9th century CE, no contemporary pre-867 CE epigraphic attestation exists.

b_mahur.first_mention_attestation: 1428 CE conquest of Mahur (Mahurgad) by Bahmani Sultan Ahmad Shah I Wali recorded in Deccan chronicles, following earlier Devagiri Yadava fortification and Puranic attestations as Matapura / Matripura.
b_mahur.etymology_analysis: Marathi vernacular contraction of Sanskrit 'Mātāpura' / 'Mātṛpura' ('City of the Mother', referencing the Renuka Devi Shakti Peetha), the historic hill-fort town in Nanded district, Maharashtra.

b_nirmal.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE epigraphy; local tradition attributes the town's founding to Nimma Nayaka (Nimma Rayudu) in the early modern period.

eponym.details: Named after 17th-century CE local ruler/founder Nimma Nayaka (Nimma Naidu / Nimma Rayudu).

b_nirmal.etymology_analysis: Nirmal is traditionally associated with local ruler Nimma Nayaka or Sanskrit 'nirmala' (pure/spotless); it has no pre-867 CE historical attestation.

b_kerimeri.first_mention_attestation: Traditional 9th-century CE attribution to Mana Naga ruler Gahilu (Manikgad / Manikgarh), though documented epigraphic references appear only by the late 12th century CE.
b_kerimeri.etymology_analysis: Manikdurg (Manikgad / Manikgarh, rendered 'Manikdrug' in the repository) derives from Manikadevi (patron goddess of the Mana Nagas) and 'durg'/'gad' (fortress). Contemporary pre-867 CE written attestation is lacking.

b_warangal.first_mention_attestation: 12th-century CE Kakatiya records under Prola II (r. c. 1116–1157 CE) and Rudradeva, who developed Orugallu (modern Warangal) alongside Anumakonda.
b_warangal.etymology_analysis: Orugallu (rendered 'Orangallu' in the repository; modern Warangal) derives from Telugu 'oru' (single) and 'kallu' (stone), meaning 'single stone/monolith', serving as the Kakatiya capital from the 12th century CE.

b_medak.first_mention_attestation: 12th-century CE Kakatiya-period construction of Medak Fort (originally named Methukudurgam, also known as Siddapuram).
b_medak.etymology_analysis: Medak derives from Telugu 'Methukudurgam' ('fort of cooked rice'), referring to the Kakatiya-era hillfortress built in the 12th century CE.

b_kollipake.first_mention_attestation: 10th–12th century CE Rashtrakuta and Western Chalukya inscriptions at Kolanupaka (including the 1125 CE Kannada inscription of Someshvara III).
b_kollipake.etymology_analysis: Kollipake (Kolanupaka / Kollipaka) derives from Telugu 'kolanu' (lake) and 'paka' (hut/settlement), flourishing as a major Jain and Shaiva center under the Rashtrakutas and Kalyani Chalukyas.

b_kaulas.first_mention_attestation: District administration tradition attributing Koulas Fort's origins to the 9th-century CE Rashtrakutas (associated with Indra IV, r. late 10th century, and Kalyani Chalukyas in the late 10th century CE).
b_kaulas.etymology_analysis: Kaulas (Koulas / Kowlas) is traditionally derived from Kailas (Kailasa Durgam); while local administration attributes the fort's origins to the 9th-century Rashtrakutas, no contemporary pre-867 CE inscription is attested.
